articles.title: Government backs British defence AI startup in $70m funding round
articles.summary:
The government has backed British defence tech startup Agon in a $70m (£53.7m) funding round, as ministers seek to reduce the UK’s reliance on overseas military technology.

The Series A round, which values the London-based company at $450m, marks the first joint investment by the government’s Sovereign AI Fund and National Security Strategic Investment Fund (NSSIF).

The round was led by venture capital firm Northzone, alongside existing investors Lakestar, Lux Capital and XYZ. Former Sequoia Capital boss Roelof Botha also joined as an investor.

Founded in January by former British Army officer Tristam Constant and Cambridge Aerospace co-founder Junaid Hussain, Agon develops software to train and test autonomous military systems.

The company is building what it describes as a “virtual battlefield”, allowing defence companies to test AI-powered systems in simulated environments rather than relying on costly physical trials.

The latest investment brings Agon’s total funding to $100m, following a $30m seed round earlier this year.

The company, which has offices in London and Berlin, will use the funding to expand its engineering and research teams and grow its work with government and defence industry customers.

“Europe is in an AI arms race as we enter the era of agentic warfare,” Constant said.

Hussain added: “Europe cannot afford to outsource the foundational AI capabilities on which its future security will depend.”

Ramping up sovereign AI investment

The investment follows an additional £140m commitment to the Sovereign AI Fund at last month’s Budget, alongside an expansion of its remit to cover robotics, autonomous systems and advanced manufacturing.

The fund typically makes equity investments of between £1m and £10m in early-stage and growing British AI companies, although the size of the government’s investment in Agon has not been disclosed.

AI minister Kanishka Narayan said: “The UK needs sovereign defence AI capabilities to bolster our national security in this new era.”

“But not only that, Britain is well-placed to lead efforts to ensure these technologies are reliable, trustworthy, and deployed responsibly.”

The funding comes amid a surge in investor appetite for European defence tech companies as governments ramp up military spending following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

European defence tech startups attracted a record $7.4bn in investment this year by October, according to figures from Dealroom and Resilience Media.

Agon co-founder Hussain’s other defence venture, Cambridge Aerospace, secured a $3.4bn valuation in August, while German defence technology firm Stark Defence has raised €500m.

A spokesperson for NSSIF said the investment demonstrated how government-backed funds could work together to “accelerate strategically important technologies” and help British companies grow.

articles.title: Poundland bidder Xyra clinches funding and plots expansion of retailer
articles.summary:
One of the frontrunners to buy Poundland has now secured full funding for its bid and is plotting to expand the discount retailer’s store footprint if it succeeds in a takeover, City AM has learned. 

Xyra Group Holdings, whose bid is being led by former BHS boss Tony Brown, will also ask the firm to extend a notice to appoint administrators to allow it to conduct due diligence, meaning the struggling retailer could face a further period in limbo.

Poundland is due to collapse into administration in the early hours of Thursday, when a notice to appoint administrators comes into effect, meaning the high street giant would likely be broken apart. 

Xyra is among four bidders racing to take over Poundland before then, alongside Irish car park-owner Martin Property Group, German investment firm Zachert Private Equity and Dubai-based wholesaler Premier Quality Foods.

Speaking publicly about Xyra’s bid for the first time, Brown told City AM: “Pending customary due diligence by identified lenders and investors, Xyra has secured interest to cover the required funding to complete the acquisition of Poundland as a going concern.” 

The little-known investment firm has presented Gordon Brothers, Poundland’s owner, with plans to widen Poundland’s estate, which currently stands at about 600 sites, by taking up new shops in areas of the UK where the investment firm believes the retailer is currently underrepresented.

Brown’s plan to boost the retailer’s performance would see the high street giant widen its number of exclusive ranges – in products like toiletries and fashion accessories – in a bid to fatten its margins, sources with knowledge of the matter told City AM.

The notice to appoint administrators, filed by Poundland’s management, blocked creditors from calling in their debts for an initial 10-day period. This was then extended and will lapse at midnight on Wednesday.

Sources close to the process had previously said there would be a “very high bar” for extending this moratorium a second time, but it is understood that Xyra Group would request this extra time for its financial backers to complete their due diligence.

Brown said: “Xyra will ask the seller for a short period of exclusivity and remains committed to its bid, which will preserve Poundland’s stores, its colleagues and its place on the high street.”

This extension would need to be triggered by Poundland’s management, who would have to apply to the courts for this to be approved. 

Poundland’s directors would be able to extend this deadline if Gordon Brothers reassured the retailer it would have access to the funds it needs to make it through these extra 10 days, people with knowledge of the discussions told City AM.

Poundland bidder plots more stores

The discount retailer has tussled with Gordon Brothers in recent weeks over claims the investment firm had been restricting its access to vital funds needed to pay suppliers and staff.

Liam Byrne MP, chair of Parliament’s business select committee, said earlier this month he had seen evidence that Poundland was being “strangled of access” to its own cash.

Gordon Brothers made two payments of about £10m each to Poundland earlier this month and is expected to release funds needed to cover the pay of the retailer’s near-12,000 staff this week.

Xyra Group Holdings is an investment vehicle led by 23-year-old entrepreneur Manvedeep Singh. The group has never previously completed an acquisition but has called upon a number of City veterans in its attempts to get its bid over the line. 

Brown, who is fronting Xyra’s bid for Poundland, has held leadership roles at retailers including Beales, BHS and Peacocks. 

A sticking point of Gordon Brothers’s attempted sale of Poundland has been its insistence that bidders cover at least part of a loan attached to the retailer, of which it holds £22.5m. Xyra has offered to pay £12.5m of this up front.

Gordon Brothers declined to comment.

articles.title: Tech stocks slide as Nvidia rally loses steam
articles.summary:
Tech stocks across Wall Street slid on Tuesday as investors pulled back from AI-linked companies following the Nvidia-fuelled rally that delivered one of the strongest trading sessions in months.

The Nasdaq Composite fell as much as 1.7 per cent in early trading before paring its losses to around 1.1 per cent, trading at 23,835 points, while the S&P 500 fell 0.4 per cent to 7,206.

Nvidia shares dropped around six per cent after the opening bell, reversing some of Monday’s 31.4 per cent surge, which restored nearly $1 trillion to the chipmaker’s market value following Jensen Huang’s surprise reinstatement as chief executive.

Other chipmakers came under pressure ahead of the opening bell, with Micron shedding more than six per cent, while AMD and Broadcom fell five per cent and four per cent respectively.

The renewed sell-off comes after the Nasdaq Composite closed 6.5 per cent higher on Monday, its 23rd biggest daily percentage gain since its inception in 1971, while the S&P 500 gained 4.7 per cent.

However, the Nasdaq remains well below its October peak, with concerns over rising interest rates, stretched technology valuations and the sustainability of AI spending continuing to weigh on investors.

Markets are also awaiting US inflation figures later this week for further indications of the Federal Reserve’s next move ahead of its December meeting.

Nvidia scrutiny continues

Huang’s reinstatement has eased some concerns over Nvidia’s leadership, but the chipmaker continues to face scrutiny over its corporate governance and financing of the wider AI industry.

His return came after Donald Trump intervened to persuade Nvidia’s board to reinstate its co-founder, less than a fortnight after he resigned following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of links to Chinese intelligence.

Trump could have personally gained as much as $15m from Monday’s Nvidia rally, according to estimates based on his financial disclosures first reported by the Financial Times, prompting Democratic senators to call for an investigation.

Nvidia is also facing forthcoming Congressional hearings and an investigation by the Securities and Exchange Commission into its accounting practices.

Spending by the world’s largest cloud computing companies is forecast to reach $1 trillion this year, rising to $1.4 trillion next year, according to figures cited by AJ Bell.

Tuesday’s losses on Wall Street contrasted with a stronger session across Asian markets, where South Korea’s Kospi jumped 6.3 per cent and Japan’s Nikkei 225 closed 3.9 per cent higher as chipmakers benefited from Monday’s US rally.

articles.title: UK firms warned on hiring workers abroad amid Russia and North Korea threat
articles.summary:
British firms have been warned about the security risks of hiring remote IT workers as the Treasury said paid work could lead to the funds being passed to North Korea and Russia. 

In a lengthy report on the financial risks facing businesses and various industries, the Treasury warned that firms risked financing hostile actors including North Korea. 

An update on national financial risks since the last report in 2021 states that remote employment of IT workers left UK firms exposed to sanctions risks. 

The Treasury’s latest assessment of proliferation financing, which is where funds or financial services support the development of destructive weapons such as nuclear arms or bio weapons, suggested that remote employment was a “cross-cutting” risk for firms across all sectors. 

North Korean workers use online freelance platforms and VPNs in order to conceal their true location, according to government officials. It means that the remote employment of IT workers could lead to funds being transferred to the country, which faces several sanctions by the UK and US, or sensitive data being shared. 

The report also warned that several North Korean nationals lived in Russia, raising the threat regarding money laundering and large-scale financial thefts. The Treasury said that the convergence of relations between Russia, North Korea and Iran through partnerships made the web of financing more hazardous for firms given sanctions could be bypassed. 

Firms’ reliance on digital services and declining levels of visibility over workers’ identities or payment flows made the UK more vulnerable. 

City minister Lucy Rigby said the UK’s status as a global financial hub “inherently exposes us to risk”. 

North Korea and Russia’s security threats

Last year, City AM reported on the rise of remote hiring practices among British firms, which looked to reduce tax burdens after a £25bn hike on employers’ National Insurance contributions. 

North Korea was recently accused of being behind a record £4.7bn hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance. 

The FBI said the attack was conducted by state-backed hacking group Tradertraitor. 

According to research in the Lowy Institute, a security think tank, state authorities take nearly all of the income generated by North Korean workers living abroad. Its report said that overseas labourers made up to an estimated $800m for the regime. Between 80 and 90 per cent of workers’ earnings are reportedly directed to the state or affiliated organisations.

Neil Carberry, chief executive of the CIPD, the industry body for human resources, said: “It’s a mistake for firms to cut costs on hiring in ways that forget that who you have in your business is at the heart of service and security. Understanding who new hires are, their skills and motivation – and even their humanity – is critical.”

articles.title: Senegal reinstated as Afcon champions after winning CAS appeal over walk-off
articles.summary:
Senegal have been reinstated as reigning champions of the Africa Cup of Nations after winning an appeal at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).

The independent panel sided with the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) over its challenge to being stripped of the title in March by the Confederation of African Football (CAF).

CAF had awarded the crown to Morocco after deeming Senegal to have forfeited the final by walking off the pitch for 14 minutes in protest at a penalty award late in the game, which they won 1-0 in January.

“After having examined the arguments raised by the Parties, the Arbitral Panel considered that the Referee’s decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority,” CAS said in a statement.

“By blowing his whistle to restart play, the Referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met – both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume.”

CAS added: “The Panel acknowledged that the Referee had to make a decision in an atmosphere of extreme tension. However, these circumstances do not justify describing the decision as ‘arbitrary’. On the contrary, the Referee’s judgment did not appear to have been affected by factors external to the game.”

How the Afcon final walk-off led to Senegal losing the title

The dispute rested on CAF’s interpretation of the Afcon rulebook. While Articles 82 and 84 of Afcon regulations state that walking off the pitch without authorisation should trigger a forfeiture, CAS that only applied in the event of the game being called off.

The FSF cited Fifa’s Laws of the Game, which say that the referee’s decision is final, and CAS agreed with that position.

The decision comes as a blow to Morocco, an increasingly influential Fifa member and co-host of the men’s World Cup in 2030, and CAF.

Senegal’s victory in the final in Rabat was an upset for the hosts and capped a chaotic and hugely contentious conclusion to the tournament.

Their players staged a walk-off when Morocco were awarded a penalty, only for Brahim Diaz to miss the spot-kick when play eventually resumed. The match went to extra time and Pape Gueye scored the only goal in the 94th minute.

CAF initially fined and suspended individual players and officials from both sides but upheld the result, yet a further appeal from Moroccan football authorities led to CAF overturning that decision and awarding Morocco a 3-0 win – and the trophy.

articles.title: ‘Act now’: MI5 urges defence firms to ramp up security amid Russia threat
articles.summary:
Britain’s intelligence service has urged firms providing support to Ukraine’s military to “act now” to defend themselves from the rising threat of Russian sabotage.

A joint alert by the Ministry of Defence (MoD) and the organisation that runs MI5’s security mission warned Russia was ramping up “attempts to conduct sabotage against European defence-related facilities”. Companies should clamp down on avenues through which Russian actors can “conduct hostile reconnaissance, and attack people, sites or operations”, they added.

“If your organisation supports military procurement or supplies equipment to Ukraine’s armed forces, it could be a target,” the MoD and National Protective Security Authority (NPSA) wrote, in what is the first time MI5 has directly accused Russia of wrongdoing. “This includes organisations in the supply chain.”

They added that Russia’s attempts to sabotage European defence-related facilities was “typically characterised by the use of proxy actors, employing low-sophistication sabotage methodologies, such as arson”.

British defence firms tied to Ukraine

Almost all Britain’s largest defence companies have in some way helped arm Ukraine’s military in its years-long war against Russia. Last week, Northern Ireland’s Thales provided over 1,000 short-range air defence missiles to the front line as part of the UK’s £240m winter support programme signed off by the MoD.

Majors including BAE Systems, Babcock and Qinetiq have also helped directly or via supply chains throughout much of the conflict, which is now in its fifth year.

Western adminsitrations have accused Russia of waging a hybrid war effort against Europe, after a string of cyber and guerrilla attacks on the region. Earlier this year, a Moscow-linked cell was held responsible for arson incidents on the home of then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer.

At the time, the Russian Embassy in London said it rejected “any attempt to associate Russia or its foreign ministry with unlawful activities”.

The alert published on Tuesday provides firms with a series of measures firms in the sector can take to minimise their exposure to any Russian sabotage efforts. Among them are steps to keep “unnecessary public information” to a minimum and adopt a “security-minded approach to communications and online activity”.

Bosses were also told to educate staff on how to recognise “hostile reconnaissance, and protect their personal security.

Louise Sandher-Jones, the armed forces minister, said: “Britain’s adversaries are not limiting themselves to military targets. They are prepared to use cyberattacks, espionage, sabotage and hostile reconnaissance against the companies, technology and supply chains that underpin our national security.”

articles.title: Asda’s £1.2bn equal pay fight enters final legal round
articles.summary:
Asda faces a potential £1.2bn payout as its equal pay battle enters its final legal stage at the Employment Tribunal this week.

The Leeds-based retailer must now prove that pay differences between its store staff and distribution centre workers are justified by reasons unrelated to sex. It follows last year’s Tribunal ruling that store roles are of equal value to those in distribution centres.

The case involves more than 60,000 Asda workers and is estimated to be worth £1.2bn. In February 2025, the Tribunal found in favour of 12 of the 14 women acting as ‘lead claimants’ for the store staff, ruling that they had established equal value with some of the lead male comparators.

This case has been ongoing since the claim was launched in 2014 and went all the way to the Supreme Court in 2021 over role comparisons, which dismissed Asda’s appeal.

This final stage trial will continue at the Manchester Employment Tribunal until 18 December, with a judgment expected later in 2027.

An Asda spokesperson said: “Asda strongly believes it can defend the pay difference because retail and distribution are two different industry sectors, each with its own market rates and distinct pay structures. It is commonplace to pay market rates in order to attract labour and has absolutely nothing to do with gender.”

Asda equal pay case part of wider retail battle

The hearing is the latest chapter in an ongoing legal battle against major British retailers over claims that predominantly female shop-floor staff are paid less than predominantly male warehouse workers.

Claimant-focused law firms Harcus Parker and Leigh Day are running separate cases against Asda, Next, Sainsbury’s, Morrisons, and the Co-op on behalf of thousands of retail employees, reportedly worth a potential £4bn.

Elsewhere in this sector-wide legal battle, the Supreme Court last month blocked Tesco from appealing a key ruling in its long-running equal pay claim brought by more than 16,000 shop workers.

Tesco had appealed through multiple courts to stop the Tribunal from using a particular definition of ‘work’, before the UK’s top court refused its application.

In September, retail giant Next won an appeal in its own equal pay claim, allowing it to pay warehouse workers more than shop-floor staff.

However, in a statement on the Employment Appeal Tribunal’s decision, Leigh Day called it a “mixed ruling”, noting that the findings that store workers performed work of equal value to warehouse operatives, yet were paid less, remained legally binding.

articles.title: Anthropic boss warns AI could wipe out 80 per cent of junior City jobs
articles.summary:
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei has warned that artificial intelligence could wipe out 80 per cent of entry-level jobs across law, consulting and finance within the next five years.

The boss of the Claude developer, which made its blockbuster Wall Street debut last week, said AI was already capable of carrying out work traditionally assigned to junior professionals.

Speaking on Fox News, Amodei warned that the technology would eliminate jobs in large numbers, with workers’ ability to use AI agents becoming increasingly important to their career prospects.

The warning goes further than his previous prediction that AI could eliminate half of entry-level white-collar jobs in the US within one to five years.

Amodei has previously described AI as a “general labour substitute for humans” and called for governments to consider measures including wage insurance and income support to cushion the impact of job losses.

Meanwhile, a Wall Street Journal profile published this week revealed that, during his time at rival OpenAI between 2016 and 2020, Amodei reportedly suggested immersive video games could help ease political unrest caused by AI-driven unemployment.

AI threatens traditional routes into the City

The warning comes amid growing concerns over graduate recruitment across Britain’s financial and professional services sectors, as businesses ramp up investment in automation.

A City AM analysis last month identified at least 137,000 job cuts or planned redundancies across major British businesses since July 2024, with around 30 per cent coming from financial, legal and professional services firms.

Barclays announced plans last month to axe some 5,000 roles globally as the FTSE 100 lender increases its use of technology and automation.

Research from Goldman Sachs in August also found that AI-related hiring pressures were disproportionately affecting junior workers, with management consulting and advertising among the industries experiencing weaker employment growth.

However, economists have cautioned against attributing Britain’s wider labour market slowdown to AI, pointing instead to rising employment costs and weaker economic growth.

PwC UK chief executive Marco Amitrano last month challenged the suggestion that AI would lead to a sustained decline in graduate recruitment across professional services.

“I don’t see a single statement of ‘AI is going to reduce the number of young people we are hiring’ as a valid statement at all,” he told the Chartered Management Institute.

The Big Four firm recruited around 1,300 entry-level workers this year, broadly in line with the previous year, although it is overhauling its graduate training programmes to reflect the growing use of AI.

articles.title: ‘Complete farce’: Welfare review won’t cut the bill as political row erupts
articles.summary:
A welfare review led by the disability minister Sir Stephen Timms has suggested that the wider system should be “replaced”, opening the prospect of new funding despite pressures on public finances. 

The Timms review on personal independence payments (Pips), which was launched after the Labour government’s U-turn on £5bn welfare cuts last year, has suggested that a system overhaul would allow for payments to “more closely reflect people’s real-life needs, additional costs and barriers”. 

Authors of the review also hailed disabled people’s “£274bn in annual spending power” while proposed changes to make the system more “personalised” were aimed at helping current claimants “participate more in society”. 

The Timms review concluded that the current Pips system was “not fit for purpose”. The government has adopted recommendations to introduce a fast-track route for people with severe, well-evidenced conditions or those who are nearing the end of life, plus reducing unnecessary award reviews for people with lifelong conditions.

Other recommendations in the review will be looked at by the government in the coming weeks. 

The review did not propose cuts to disability benefits, putting it on a collision course with Alan Milburn’s ideas in his review on curbing youth unemployment levels last week. 

It also did not demand a tightening in eligibility nor a conditionality on cash awards, as City AM revealed on the weekend. 

Extra incentives “signposting to education, employment or peer support schemes” does not have to be taken up by claimants under the review’s proposals. 

Burnham’s £41bn welfare challenge

Burnham is under pressure to deliver savings rapidly in order to stick to the government’s fiscal rules, keep borrowing costs down and meet investment targets in areas such as defence and health. The Prime Minister has said he wanted to get the “welfare bill down…in a Labour way.”

Total spending on Pip this yea ris forecast to be £32.1bn and could reach £41.5bn in 2030. Anxiety and depression are the fasts growing grounds for claiming.

The Milburn report recommended about £4bn in benefit cuts for under 25-year-olds through a reset of the system and how cash is distributed, complemented by about £6bn in extra employment investment to help young people into work. 

A contrast between the two reports could set the government up for a difficult dilemma in welfare reforms across different age groups and for juggling financial pressures.

Timms said that the initial changes “are a first step to building a system which gives greater security for those with the most severe conditions”. 

Labour is ‘the welfare party’

But shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said the review was a “complete farce” after Sir Keir Starmer, Andy Burnham’s predecessor in Downing Street, abandoned initial cuts following a revolt from Labour backbenchers. 

“Labour’s flagship review into sickness benefits has failed,” Whately said. 

“Labour will never cut welfare because they are the welfare party, and their left-wing backbenchers will never let them.

“The Conservatives will review the entire PIP system, remove eligibility for low-level mental health Pip claims, rapidly assess hundreds of thousands of additional claims and get Britain working again.”

Whately added that the review’s recommendations would lead to greater spending and fewer checks on claimants. 

The review’s co-chair Sharon Brennan, who is a health charity director, said: “Disabled people contribute £274bn in annual spending power and make highly valued contributions to society, this should be recognised and supported by a new benefit that will hope will also no longer feel dehumanising to claim.”

articles.title: Waste in defence spending ‘slightly worse’ despite looming threat of war
articles.summary:
Defence officials have admitted that waste in large contracts for weaponry has got “worse” despite the possibility of Russia launching a war against a Nato country by 2030.  

Senior figures at the Ministry of Defence defended their running of large contracts for weapons and other essential equipment even if delivery of key programmes had deteriorated.

Speaking to MPs on the Defence Committee, the National Armaments Director, Rupert Pearce, said the wider scale of programmes being delivered on time and within budgets showed “the system isn’t broken”. 

“We’re talking about the most challenging programmes that one can run – multi-decade programmes for very large platforms that are extremely complex, and trying to keep us at the cutting edge of capability,” Pearce said. 

“I don’t think we should conclude that we’re a lot worse than anybody else and the system is broken.”

However, he admitted that troubles in the department around large procurement was “slightly worse” in a short answer to a question on whether programmes “remained in trouble”.

‘Red rating’

The Ministry of Defence is under significant pressure to better manage its finances after receiving orders to save about £10.7bn cumulatively between 2026 and 2030. 

The department has faced years of questions over mis-expenditure and failed projects, including through General Dynamics’ Ajax programme for semi-autonomous armoured vehicles that is facing nearly a decade of delay and public spending of over £5bn. 

A National Audit Office review found that, of 20 projects that were in the government’s major projects portfolio, eight were handed a “red” rating. 

Other than the Ajax programme, other projects around submarines, warships and tanks are also labelled as being “unachievable”.

At the same time, officials are tasked with ramping up investment and procurement on arms after German defence officials suggested Russia could attack a Nato country by 2029. Defence secretary Wes Streeting has called for the UK to be ready for war in a 1000 days by building up arms and security systems in order to deter attacks. 

Defence officials rely on ‘Herculean’ targets

Emma Lewwell, the Labour MP for South Shields on the parliamentary committee, warned that Pearce’s admission that the UK was “not terrible” on delivery for large programmes was still “not good”. 

The armaments chief responded by saying that multi-billion pound projects could have remedies, including greater cash injections or a reset. 

Pearce argued that officials were “not  looking to overspend” or “profligate with other people’s money in defence” although pressures on budgets could lead to “Herculean” assumptions that would later be shown to be unrealistic. 

“It’s not an easy game, but we need to be a lot more conservative about what things cost,” Pearce said. 

Procurement chiefs in the department are also coming under pressure after reports in the Financial Times suggested that the UK bought fake plastic explosives for Ukraine. The MoD said it had “robust procurement processes in place”.

On Tuesday, the MI5 also issued a new alert stating that UK defence firms were at increased threat of firebombing and other attacks by Russia.

It said proxies for the Kremlin were behind sabotage plots against top companies across Europe.

“In recent months Russia has increased attempts to conduct sabotage against European defence-related facilities,” the warning said.

“If your organisation supports military procurement or supplies equipment to Ukraine’s armed forces, it could be a target. This includes organisations in the supply chain. Act now to reduce opportunities for hostile actors to identify your organisation or people as targets, conduct hostile reconnaissance and attack people, sites or operations.”

articles.title: Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond: But Fleming’s real 007 will never reach the screen
articles.summary:
Most of you will know by now that Amazon MGM Studios has cast Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond. He will be the seventh incarnation within the official 007 canon, and is inevitably a controversial choice, although honestly, no-one would have been uncontroversial. There was the familiar apoplexy at the ritual suggestion that Bond could be a woman, or non-white (Rege-Jean Page, John Boyega and 54-year-old Sir Idris Elba were touted). One very meta hypothesis said that “007” was merely a codename and that the new bearer need not be James Bond at all.

Dr No and the first Bond premiere

The seven-year gap between No Time To Die and Bond 26 will be the longest hiatus in the franchise since the first film, Dr No, opened on Friday 5 October 1962. No-one knew if an adaptation of Ian Fleming’s solidly selling espionage thrillers would be a success, and the budget was only $1.1m (in Hollywood terms, between $15m and $20m today). The premiere reflected that: apart from the cast, the stars were Fleming himself, La Dolce Vita star Anita Ekberg and 88-year-old writer and former intelligence officer Somerset Maugham, whose refined but damaged hero Ashenden, reporting to a superior known only as R, had been an obvious influence on Fleming.

It was the same day that the Beatles released their first single, Love Me Do.

Christopher Nolan and the period Bond reboot

One possibility raised during the current interregnum was to reboot the franchise by making the next film in the period of the novels and Fleming’s life, 1953 to 1964. Three years ago, Sir Christopher Nolan was reportedly talking to Bond producer Barbara Broccoli about directing the next “two or three” films in the franchise; but one of his conditions was that they would be faithful, in-period adaptations of the novels.

Nolan had previously said it would be “an amazing privilege” to direct a Bond film, but acknowledged that “you’re working with a particular set of constraints”. The constraint he had set himself was too much, and no deal was agreed. It was not the first time the idea of going back in time has been aired: it was mooted as soon as everything was in place for No Time To Die. And it would certainly be a dramatic departure for a franchise which depends on familiar building blocks – high-tech hi-jinks, modern glamour and a degree of irony.

So what would a period Bond look like? If we take the hero of Fleming’s first (and I think best) novel, Casino Royale, how would a 1953-vintage 007 present himself to us?

Ian Fleming’s James Bond in Casino Royale

Commander James Bond, Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve, is six feet tall, taut and wiry rather than muscle-bound. He has black hair, a comma-shaped lock of which falls over his forehead, and cold, blue-grey eyes; the three-inch scar down his right cheek completes a severe appearance. You don’t get many laughs.

He is in his mid-thirties, and, of course, a veteran of the Second World War. His naval commission was a convenient cover which he has maintained, ending the War a commander; the shadowy brutality we come to see in Bond is deeply practised and inhaled.

Did he take part in the commando raids? On the Lofoten Islands, Vagsoy or Haugesund in Norway? He is entirely at home on skis, a legacy of his Scottish father and Swiss mother, who were killed in a climbing accident in the Aiguilles Rouges when he was 11. Bond has the closed-off self-sufficiency of the orphan, case-hardened by boarding school: he was removed from Eton after a year – “some alleged trouble with one of the boys’ maids” – and sent to Fettes in Edinburgh. When he left at 17, he’d been taught duty and sacrifice, and had boxed for the school.

Smoking, drinking and the Vesper martini

This tough athleticism has kept Bond going. He still carries that fatalism of wartime, because in a sense the War has never ended for him. The adversaries are different but death tastes the same in any cuisine. He smokes, like most men in the 1950s, but 60 or 70 cigarettes a day is recklessness. You notice the aroma about him straight away. The mixture of Turkish and Balkan tobacco, with a very high nicotine content, doesn’t dissipate. You may find the smell refined, luxurious – but it’s with Bond all day, getting stronger and stronger.

He is enthusiastic about food, but part of you wonders how he can taste anything. And if he does, how can he remember? His drinking is as reckless as his smoking.

“I take a ridiculous pleasure in what I eat and drink,” he once said.

You can’t argue with the second part. He favours a martini, of course, or a Vesper, his own twist on it. All you can say is it seems a lot of liquor going into one glass. When he travels, which is often, he prefers to drink locally: mint juleps in Kentucky, Sazeracs in New Orleans, Rum Collins in the Bahamas. But he also likes champagne – Taittinger is a favourite – and bourbon and Scotch. There’s a souring sense of it keeping demons tamped down, and a man who drinks such quantities of hard booze always has a sharp tang about him.

A hero who is hard to like

In truth, 007 is hard work as a conversationalist. He revels in a brutal honesty, tearing away your illusions and comforting euphemisms as well as having none of his own. He hates, fears, sentimentality.

“Yes, dammit, I said ‘was’. The bitch is dead now.”

He’s been hurt badly, grievously, you can tell that. His attitude to women shows the pain. They are disposable luxuries, most of the thrill being in the chase. If they have feelings too, Bond gives no sign of noticing. Pain can make people hard or soft. With Bond, he wants everyone to share.

Do you like the man? No, it’s very hard to like him. He’s hard and cold, his smooth, public-school voice all clipped consonants and efficient vowels. He gives little away, and has few stories he can tell you. He excels at what he does, and it has to be done, but it’s a job which does nothing to breathe warmth into a man’s chilly nature.

Could a James Bond reboot ever work?

It makes you wonder whether even a film-maker of Nolan’s gifts could package this protagonist, remaining faithful to the source material but giving him popular appeal. Fleming’s Bond isn’t an anti-hero, Fleming was too much part of the Establishment for that, but he’s an invitation to understand that the rough men who stand ready to do violence while we sleep peacefully are just that: rough. They haven’t the luxury to be anything else.

It won’t happen. But there’s little doubt that a period Bond, soured by life and haunted by grief, would be a more challenging and more fascinating cinematic artefact than a 26th iteration of the existing formula. There’s a reason we talk about the Bond franchise, though. Part of the deal is that it stays the same.

articles.title: Google snaps up King’s Cross office as AI giants expand London footprint
articles.summary:
Google has agreed to buy a major office building in King’s Cross as the US tech behemoth expands its London property portfolio and strengthens its AI operations in the capital.

The search giant is acquiring 6 Pancras Square from BNP Paribas Asset Management Alts and Canadian pension investor PSP Investments for an undisclosed sum.

The building comprises 371,000 sq ft of prime office space and a further 32,000 sq ft of retail accommodation across six units.

The acquisition comes a decade after Google moved into King’s Cross and will form part of its wider London campus alongside its Central Saint Giles offices and sprawling Platform 37 headquarters.

“Our purchase of 6 Pancras Square sends a clear signal of our long-term commitment to the UK,” said Kate Alessi, Google’s UK and Ireland managing director.

“This investment ensures our UK teams can continue building world-changing AI, driving innovation, and contributing to the growth of the country’s economy.”

The deal builds on Google’s £5bn investment programme in Britain, which includes its Waltham Cross data centre.

The sellers acquired the building through a joint venture in 2013, before King’s Cross established itself as one of London’s most sought-after office districts.

John O’Driscoll, global co-head of real estate at BNP Paribas Asset Management Alts, said the investors had delivered “strong income growth and value appreciation” over their 13-year ownership of the building.

Kings cross draws more AI giants

Google’s acquisition comes just a day after it was reported that Microsoft was preparing to relocate to nearby Belgrove House, a 180,000 sq ft office building left vacant after pharmaceutical giant Merck abandoned plans for a £1bn UK investment.

Property agents estimate Microsoft could pay around £27m in annual rent for the building, having already agreed to lease the entirety of Film House in Soho earlier this year to accommodate its growing British AI teams.

King’s Cross has attracted a string of major tech companies in recent years, with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Deepmind and autonomous vehicle developer Wayve establishing operations in the area.

In September, $9bn AI coding startup Replit picked King’s Cross for its first international office, while vaccine maker Moderna announced plans earlier this month to relocate its UK commercial headquarters to the nearby Tribeca development.

The influx of tech companies has helped fuel demand for prime London office space, with research from property consultancy CBRE forecasting that AI firms could occupy as much as 4m sq ft across the capital by 2033, up from 1.5m sq ft earlier this year.

London has attracted 86 AI-related foreign direct investment projects since the beginning of 2025, according to figures reported in September by fDi Markets, more than Paris and Madrid combined.

The purchase price has not been disclosed in either announcement.

articles.title: Nations Championship: Rugby onto a good thing by borrowing from football
articles.summary:
This weekend over 150,000 fans will be at Twickenham for the inaugural Nations Championship finals weekend, a three-day rugby extravaganza with some blockbuster fixtures. But it won’t be a sell-out.

The novel spectacle of three back-to-back double-headers, with plenty of empty seats, will provoke much debate about the merits of rugby’s new North v South global tournament.

But, just like their football counterparts at Uefa, who formed the Nations League back in 2019, the 10 leading rugby nations who united to create the Nations Championship are onto a good thing. And like Uefa, they just need to finesse the concept, maybe rethink the finals weekend, and let it establish itself with players and fans.

The idea dates back a few years, with Sir Bill Beaumont a key exponent when chairman of World Rugby. It gathered momentum with Tom Harrison, a key figure behind The Hundred, at the helm as CEO of Six Nations Rugby.

Enter the Nations Championship and the recent formation of F10, a shrewd commercial venture uniting the 10 leading Northern and Southern Hemisphere nations to collectively sell rights, maximise revenues and accelerate the growth of international rugby.  

How rugby is following the Nations League playbook

The similarities between football’s Nations League and rugby’s Nations Championship are many.

Both were designed to maximise commercial value for their sports in an increasingly competitive world by solving a similar problem: international matches outside major tournaments lacked a compelling competitive narrative.

The answer they’ve both come up with is to turn the existing slate of international matches into a structured competition with a title at stake, driving greater fan engagement and squeezing another round of fixtures into the calendar while they’re about it.

The result is more meaningful fixtures, with every game contributing to an overall championship, and a grand final.

Great for fans who want competitive matches to watch, a league table to look at, and a trophy to aim for.

Great for TV companies, who get a recurring, branded tournament, making for a more commercially attractive broadcast proposition. So much so that ITV was prepared to pay a reported £90m for the rights to the 2026 and 2028 Nations Championships.

For F10, from 2030 onwards, this creates the prospect of a lucrative global rights deal with a major streaming platform, or driving up the price domestic broadcasters like ITV must pay to keep Netflix and the like at bay.

And great, too, for sponsors. The increased significance of these tournament formats increases exposure and engagement for existing commercial partners, while adding a whole new package of commercial inventory for Uefa and F10 to market.

Rugby got unlucky with the collapse of the Qatar Airways title sponsorship of the Nations Championship, which went by the wayside due to the unrest in the Middle East. But the success of this year’s inaugural “proof of concept”, delivering some momentous matches and truly memorable moments, has established a compelling global sponsorship opportunity for future years.

Nations Championship has a global advantage

Where the Nations Championship differs from football’s Nations League is in its global nature, with the potential to take finals weekend around the world for an even grander finale.

A future edition of the finals weekend in the Middle East or North America seems inevitable. Especially when you consider that both the men’s and women’s Rugby World Cups are taking place in the US, in 2031 and 2033 respectively.

It might mean an even bigger challenge than filling Twickenham this weekend, but the opportunity to use the Nations Championship to grow rugby in a major market like the US represents perhaps the most lucrative path for rugby to follow football’s commercial playbook.

Henry Chappell is founder and chief executive of marketing agency Pitch.

articles.title: Oil prices fall as traders weigh hopes of Iran talks against shipping risks
articles.summary:
Oil prices extended their decline on Tuesday as hopes of potential deal between the US and Iran offset shipping risks in the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude slipped 0.4 per cent to $88.9 per barrel in early trading, after closing at its lowest level since 31 August on Monday.

West Texas Intermediate also declined 0.2 per cent to $79.9 per barrel, after hitting its lowest level since 26 August.

The pullback marks a sharp reversal from earlier risk-driven rallies. Analysts credited the prospect of possible negotiations with the unwinding of the “geopolitical risk premium” built into crude prices.

Ewa Manthey, commodities strategist at ING, said: “The prospect of negotiations has eased some immediate concerns over Middle East supply, particularly as crude exports from the Persian Gulf have remained relatively resilient despite continued disruption around the Strait of Hormuz. 

“However, significant differences between the US and Iran remain, leaving oil vulnerable to any setback in talks.”

Maritime flashpoints

Despite potential movement in diplomatic negotiations, threats to trade in the strait remain elevated.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard navy said three “violating” oil tankers caught fire in the strait on Monday after hitting naval mines. 

Meanwhile, the US is investigating whether Iran was involved in cyberattacks on as many as 50 energy tankers, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Fragile market

Rising production away from the Middle East, including in Brazil and Guyana, alongside the reopening of Libya’s pipeline and temporary US waivers on Russian oil sanctions  has replenished global stockpiles.

But analysts warned against treating lower prices as a sign the market is in a complete recovery.

In a client note, Daniel Hynes, senior commodity strategist at ANZ, said: “Despite some improvement in inventories and product availability, the oil market remains under severe strain.

“Oil prices… and investor positioning increasingly suggest the market expects conditions to normalise. Yet logistics remain constrained and inventory buffers are thin. 

“The oil system therefore appears to be moving from acute scarcity towards persistent vulnerability, rather than returning to normal.”

articles.title: Manchester City owner’s Mubadala and Brit Bake launch UAE SailGP team
articles.summary:
British investor Chris Bake has joined forces with sovereign wealth fund Mubadala, chaired by Manchester City owner Sheikh Mansour, to enter a UAE team in SailGP.

Bake is already a part-owner of the British team, Emirates GBR, which won the SailGP Championship last year, while Mubadala Capital has owned the Brazilian team since 2024.

The UAE SailGP team will become the 14th in the fleet when it joins the series in 2027 and will be led by Brit Hannah Mills, who is leaving Emirates GBR after five years.

“The UAE SailGP Team has been a long-standing ambition for SailGP and our partners in the region,” said CEO and co-founder Sir Russell Coutts.

“It reflects how deep that relationship has become, and our commitment for many years to come. It’s a privilege to expand our relationship with Chris Bake and Mubadala Capital – their continued support says a great deal about the trust our owners and partners have in this championship and where it’s heading.”

Mubadala Capital is the asset management subsidiary of Mubadala Investment Company, which is chaired by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al Nahyan and run by Manchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak.

“The UAE SailGP Team is a significant milestone in our relationship with SailGP and for the nation more broadly,” said Mubadala Capital chief operating officer Fatima Al Noaimi.

“[It’s] a team for the country to get behind, and a reason for the next generation of Emiratis to see themselves on the world’s fastest racecourse.”

SailGP season finale in Abu Dhabi

The announcement comes ahead of this weekend’s season finale, being held in Abu Dhabi, where Australian team Bonds Flying Roos are favourites to take the title.

“I have huge belief in SailGP’s trajectory, and in the unique power of sailing, especially for young people,” said Bake, a former energy and commodities trader and chairman of Vitol.

“The opportunity to build this team alongside Mubadala Capital – in a country with the ambition to lead in everything it takes on – is a privilege.”

articles.title: FCA threatens action against tech firms offering unauthorised AI finance
articles.summary:
The City watchdog has warned tech giants and social media platforms that it “will not hesitate” to intervene if their AI tools offer financial services without regulatory approval.

In a new statement, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) set out its expectations for companies developing AI agents – tools capable of making decisions and carrying out tasks on behalf of consumers.

The watchdog warned that as AI moves beyond offering financial advice to making payments, arranging loans and managing investments, more technology firms could require its approval to operate in the UK.

“Just because a business describes itself as a technology provider does not mean that they do not need to be authorised by us to provide financial services in the UK,” the FCA said.

“We have powers to intervene if we believe regulated financial services are being offered without our authorisation and will not hesitate to use them if necessary.”

The regulator urged tech companies to engage with it before launching new products, warning that consumers could be left without protection or compensation if things go wrong.

This comes as more Brits turn to AI to manage their finances, with FCA research published earlier this year finding around 11m UK adults would be willing to let the technology make financial decisions within agreed limits.

Previous research also found 40 per cent of young investors mistakenly believed chatbots were regulated by the FCA.

City bosses held accountable for AI

The watchdog has also made it clear that financial services firms and their senior managers remain responsible for the AI tools they use, even if another company develops the technology.

Bosses were warned to understand how much freedom they give AI systems to make decisions, what risks they pose, and how they can intervene if something goes wrong.

Banks and other financial firms have also been told to consider whether to accept payments made by AI agents on behalf of customers, and who would be liable if mistakes were made.

Meanwhile, consumers have been urged to exercise caution when sharing bank details with AI tools and consider setting spending limits or requiring approval for every transaction.

The statement follows warnings from FCA chief executive Nikil Rathi last month that rapid advances in technology were putting risks to Britain’s financial markets “on steroids”.

However, the watchdog has maintained that existing financial regulations apply to AI, rather than drawing up a separate set of rules for the technology.

The FCA will also launch a new initiative bringing together financial services firms, policymakers and technology companies to help develop and safely test new AI products.

“AI is redefining financial services,” the watchdog said.

“Deployed well, AI can increase productivity, improve competition, services and drive economic growth.”

articles.title: Has UK reached peak Guinness? Far from it, says pub boss
articles.summary:
The so-called end to the Guinness boom has been exaggerated, a top pub boss has insisted, as he claimed punters are reaching for pints of the black stuff in droves.

Simon Dodd, chief executive of London pub group Young’s, has taken to social media to defend the Irish stout from claims that it has been overtaken by fruit lagers like Jubel as Gen-Zs favourite tipple.

Last month, it appeared Guinness’s rapid rise over the last few years was approaching its end after Fuller’s boss Simon Emeny said Jubel – along with premium lager Asahi – is growing at a faster rate. 

The Irish stout had seen double-digit growth at Fuller’s pubs for five consecutive years but this trend is now “slowing down quite significantly and becoming more normalised,” he told City AM.

Dodd appeared to back up this warning a few days later, saying that sales of Guinness had dropped off in favour of lagers, including former Top Gear host Jeremy Clarkson’s Hawkstone.

Diageo, the FTSE 100 firm which owns Guinness, reported that sales of the stout had declined by “low single-digits” between July and September.

Guinness ‘remains a powerhouse’

But the Young’s boss has now rushed to soothe fears that the black stuff is going out of fashion. In a post to LinkedIn, Dodd insisted that plummeting temperatures mean Guinness is “growing again”. 

He added that sales of Guinness at Young’s’s army of pubs were in fact higher than the same period last year, boosted by the expanded Autumn international rugby calendar.

He said: “Well, the weather finally turned crisp and the Autumn Nations Series kicked off. The result? Guinness bounced straight back into growth.

“Sales have seen strong volume growth over the last few weeks, adding thousands of extra pints compared to last year. It remains a powerhouse brand for us, and working closely with the team to drive the draught category forward continues to pay off.

“There’s plenty of room for great brands on the bar, sometimes the British weather just dictates the pour!”

Guinness is not the first consumer favourite to have reached a so-called peak in recent years. Greggs boss Roisin Currie has insisted in recent months that the UK has not reached “peak sausage roll” after the bakery giant faced slowing sales.

The Newcastle-based bakery chain is targeting at least 3,500 sites in the UK, from its current footprint of 2,796, though the group recently announced plans to cut 740 jobs as it closes a string of factories.

In November last year, former Domino’s boss Andrew Rennie left the takeaway giant shortly after declaring that the company had reached “peak pizza” and would instead lurch sideways into fried chicken.

His successor Nicola Frampton, however, has doubled down on the case for a disciplined expansion into chicken. “Chicken is a large adjacent category. We can enter it using our existing system rather than building a new one,” she said in August.

articles.title: B&Q owner Kingfisher targets higher profit as Screwfix soars
articles.summary:
B&Q owner Kingfisher has lifted its profit target for the second time in just two months after seeing its shift towards trade customers drive demand at Screwfix.

The FTSE 100 home improvements retailer told shareholders it now expects to notch a pre-tax profit of between £610m and £640m, having lifted its target range to between £595m and £635m only in September.

Kingfisher, whose chief executive Thierry Garnier will depart at the end of the year, has looked towards trade customers – including plumbers and electricians – in a bid to grow its sales. 

The group said Screwfix, which operates at 943 sites in the UK, has “significantly outperformed the market” in the last three months, helped by growth in its number of customers and the volume of sales.

Kingfisher said growing demand has been driven by its new trade-focused ranges of electrical products, plumbing gear and power tools. The retailer has seen “continued momentum” in its loyalty programme, which was launched in October last year.

On a like-for-like basis, sales at Screwfix grew by 6.9 per cent in the third quarter, better than 5.6 per cent growth in the first half of the year.

B&Q, on the other hand, suffered a one per cent drop-off in like-for-like sales, though this was a softer decline than the 1.8 per cent recorded in the second quarter. Kingfisher said the retailer has seen improving sales of painting products and garden power tools.

Kingfisher boss heads for door

The group posted a 2.8 per cent sales decline in France, where it operates the Castorama and Brico Depot retail brands. The latter has suffered from “weaker demand in building materials and larger project categories,” Kingfisher said.

Analysts at stockbroker Panmure Liberum said the group’s growing sales in the UK are “encouragingly” being backed up by “improving trends elsewhere”.

This reduces Kingfisher’s “reliance on any meaningful French recovery where performance has been resilient given the poor economic backdrop,” they added.

Garnier said: “We delivered a solid quarter, with continued market share gains and strong momentum across our strategic growth drivers of trade, e-commerce and marketplace. This gives us the confidence to upgrade our guidance.”

The Kingfisher chief executive announced his departure in May, after being poached by Dutch supermarket group Ahold Delhaize. He will be replaced by Sebastian Gundel, who had been the boss of German DIY retailer OBI.

Garnier added: “We are building a stronger, more resilient Kingfisher and are well positioned to capitalise on the opportunities ahead. 

“I want to thank all our colleagues for the energy and commitment they continue to bring to Kingfisher every day. I am incredibly proud to have been part of that team.”

Shares in Kingfisher dipped by 3.6 per cent in early trading to 376p. The stock has gained nearly 19 per cent in the year to date.

articles.title: AO boss: ‘The Chancellor gave Brits £100 off energy bills, I’m giving them £3,000’
articles.summary:
The boss of AO World has taken on the Chancellor’s energy bill handout with his company’s expansion into solar, which he claims will blow Healey’s support out of the water.

John Roberts, chief executive of the electricals retailer, said the group’s launch of solar panels will offer households a full package at £5,500, below the market rate of £8,500.

Taking aim at the Chancellor’s Budget, which he described as “an hour of not a lot”, Roberts said his company’s new venture will do more to take the pressure off of cash-strapped Brits.

He said: “The Chancellor gave households £100 towards their electricity bill. I’m giving them £3,000 – through the discount relative to market price of what we’re giving them in solar.”

John Healey’s headline announcement at the Budget – a £100 rebate on energy bills for about 20m households – will “run out in about 11 or 12 days – there goes a few billion,” Roberts said. 

He added: “I’m not sure [the Budget] dealt with anything. It was an hour of not a lot. Ultimately, if you look at the country through a business lens, we have to be focussed on our cost base as much as we are looking after our people, and we’ve got to do things better at lower cost.

“I want to stay absolutely focused on what I’m in control of, and what I’m in control of is delivering amazing value for customers, and we will continue to do that.”

Shares dip after profit downgrade

AO World will launch in solar panels in the next twelve months, before following this up with EV charging and air conditioning. 

This new venture will allow the retailer to use the infrastructure it already has for appliance installations, Roberts said.

“When you look at the narrative of energy security for people, solar is going to become more important for people.

“We are good as an organisation at doing very difficult things in and around people’s homes, doing them to a very high standard, and doing that at scale on a national basis, and so we have that infrastructure all in place.”

AO World, which also operates a mobile network and sells electrical goods, grew its pre-tax profit by a fifth in the six months to the end of September, to £21.5m.

The group saw revenue jump by six per cent to £617.5m and said it is “well-positioned” for Christmas trading, though Roberts said the company has “flagged” to its shareholders a drop-off in consumer confidence in recent weeks.

He said the retailer has seen “a slight deterioration in consumer behavior and consumers trading down on value” in the last six weeks. “We’re just flagging a note of caution for the second half,” he said.

The group lowered its pre-tax profit target to a range of £48m to £54m, having previously said in June that it was on track to meet consensus targets of about £54.7m.

Shares in AO World dipped by more than eight per cent in early trading, to 84.5p, as investors were spooked by the warnings of a softer second half.

articles.title: FTSE 100 giant Compass confirms plans to ditch main London listing for New York
articles.summary:
Catering giant Compass has become the latest London firm set to switch its main listing to New York, dealing another heavy blow to the UK’s public markets.

The group will hold a shareholder consultation over a move of its primary listing to the US, while retaining a secondary listing in the UK. A potential switch could take effect in 2028, subject to shareholder approval.

Compass’ board said it “believes that the United States has become the natural long-term listing venue for Compass”, better aligning “its capital markets presence” with the group’s geographical profile.

Ian Meakins, chair of Compass, said: “Over the past decade, North America has become a powerful engine of growth for Compass and today accounts for the majority of revenue and profit. It is home to our largest client base and more than half of our people.”

The region accounts for 75 per cent of operating profit, while 325,000 of its 600,000 strong global workforce is present in the US. The firm also opted to switch the trading currency of its shares from sterling to US dollars in April to appeal to international investors.

Meakins added that the UK “remains an important market”, where it continues to see “significant opportunities for growth”. It has been listed in London since 1988.

But the move is a further blow to the struggling London Stock Exchange, which has seen a flurry of high-profile departures in recent years.

UK-founded fintech Wise, Paddy Power owner Flutter and equipment rental firm Ashstead are among those who have recently ditched primary listings in London in favour of New York. 

Surging revenue

Compass’ revenue increased 9.3 per cent over the course of the financial year, jumping from $46.5bn (£35.6bn) to $50.8bn. 

The rise was credited to a boost in business activity in the second half of the year. The group won $4.4bn in new contracts, a 16 per cent year on year rise, while retaining 96 per cent of its existing clients.

Operating profit also increased 13 per cent to $3.4bn, pushing operating margins up slightly to 7.4 per cent.

Earnings per share also rose 12 per cent to 148p, while the catering giant confirmed a dividend of 74p, up from 65.9p the prior year.

Kickstarting share buyback

Compass invested $4.4bn in capital expenditure and M&A, strengthening its “capabilities and growth prospects”. But the firm also confirmed its expansion into European markets is “largely completed” and expects acquisition spend to begin to slow. 

It plans to turn its efforts towards restarting its share buyback programme, returning up to $1.5bn to shareholders over the next two years.

The group anticipates high single-digit operating profit growth in the next financial year, driven by revenue growth of seven per cent.

Dominic Blakemore, group chief executive, said: “These results demonstrate the power of our recurring revenue model, unmatched scale and market leadership in a large and highly fragmented industry.

“We remain a proudly international business, committed to the UK, and to investing in the attractive growth opportunities across all our markets.”

articles.title: Asian tech stocks surge on Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia
articles.summary:
Asian tech stocks surged during Tuesday trading after Jensen Huang’s unexpected reinstatement as chief executive of Nvidia sent investors rushing back to markets.

South Korea’s Kospi jumped 6.3 per cent to above 5,000 points, a sharp reversal from last week’s extended losses.

Index heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, both key suppliers of memory chips, increased as much as 8.2 per cent and 8.5 per cent. The two chipmakers account for roughly half of the Kospi’s market capitalisation.

In Japan, the tech-heavy Nikkei 225 jumped 3.9 per cent, lifted by semiconductor firm Advantest and Tokyo Electron which rose 12.4 per cent and 7.6 per cent respectively.

The broader Topix also increased 2.3 per cent.

Taiwan extended Monday’s gains, after TSMC soared almost 10 per cent, approaching the maximum daily trading limit. Nvidia accounts for nearly a fifth of revenue at TSMC, which is the world’s largest chip foundry. The Taiex also increased 8.9 per cent.

Wall Street blitz

The race back to chipmakers and tech stocks across Asia was triggered by the biggest one-day jump for stocks on Wall Street since Trump’s ‘liberation day’ tariff blitz in April 2025.

The S&P 500 index closed 4.7 per cent higher, while the Nasdaq 100 jumped 6.9 per cent. Futures tracking both indices point to them rising 0.3 per cent when US markets open on Tuesday.

Nvidia’s share price rocketed 31.4 per cent to $165 on Monday, while it added nearly $1 trillion in market capitalisation. But the price is still around five per cent lower than it was on 11 November, the day of Huang’s resignation.

Other tech stocks also recorded a boost in share price. Intel jumped 16.3 per cent to $59.6, while Micron rose 19 per cent to $133.1.

“Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as CEO is the most significant development for the AI trade in recent weeks, removing a major source of uncertainty for Nvidia and the wider industry,” said Stephen Yiu, chief investment officer at Blue Whale.

“His return provides reassurance to the market that the company can continue without the shift in strategy that a change in leadership might have brought, particularly given the deep relationships Huang has built with customers and suppliers and his central role in shaping and financing the wider AI ecosystem.”

Copper also rebounded sharply, climbing above $5.6 per pound yesterday, but has since lost its Nvidia-driven gains, falling three per cent as focus shifted back to Chinese demand.

Ewa Manthey, commodities strategist at ING, said: “The latest weakness is largely a financial market story rather than a broad deterioration in copper fundamentals.

“The Chinese physical market remains tight, with elevated import premiums and nearby spreads signalling limited availability. Some of the copper accumulated in the US earlier this year is beginning to return to the international market, but this should take time to materially ease tightness elsewhere.”

Trump steps in

Widespread surges across US markets followed Huang’s return to Nvidia, just days after the board initially rejected his offer to return to the chipmaker. 

His reinstatement also came less than two weeks after he was forced to resign over reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese spy.

The company came under pressure by US president Donald Trump to reappoint Huang, and on Monday Trump said he “made a deal” to “convince” the tech giant’s board to bring him back and downplayed concerns over national security.

Speaking to CNBC, Trump said: “They did ask for reassurance on the national security threat.

“We gave them assurances at least with everything we know, and we know a lot.”

articles.title: Back with a Huang: Jensen reinstated as Nvidia chief exec after Trump call
articles.summary:
Stock markets were stunned on Monday after one of the best-known tech executives on the planet staged a shock return following a direct intervention from the US president. 

Billionaire Jensen Huang, who resigned as chief executive of chipmaker Nvidia earlier this month following reports of multiple extra-marital relationships with colleagues and an alleged Chinese spy, was reinstated just days later despite his actions triggering an internal investigation and an external probe by the US FBI.

In a stock exchange statement on Monday afternoon, the board of Nvidia said it had decided “unanimously” to reappoint Huang immediately following assurances from “senior levels” of the US government that “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

US President Donald Trump, who appeared to take credit for the decision and reportedly joined an Nvidia boardroom call ahead of the announcement, said it was “the correct and proper decision,” adding that the US government “did not possess evidence” that Huang engaged in unlawful conduct.

“I’m doing it for the country…. if I didn’t get involved you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come,” he said in a lengthy interview with CNBC.

Huang ‘honoured’ to return to Nvidia

Huang, famed for his avant-garde leather jackets, said he was “honoured” to return to the company.

“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process… I can’t wait to get back to work,” he said.

Nvidia shares rocketed as much as 32 per cent following the announcement, clawing back most of the more than $1 trillion in market value the tech firm had haemorrhaged since Huang’s sudden exit in one of the most dramatic comebacks in corporate history. Chipmaker peers joined in on the rally, with Intel shares jumping 13 per cent and UK-based Arm soaring 17 per cent. 

“Jensen Huang is the Rocky Balboa of the stock market. He’s taken a huge hit, been knocked down, and then climbed straight back into the ring,” says Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell.

“This is the biggest corporate U-turn in living memory. To go from being embroiled in a spy scandal to being reinstated as the head of one of the world’s most valuable companies in less than a fortnight is nothing short of remarkable.”

Huang’s return to Nvidia’s board comes despite repeated reports that board members had ruled out the possibility of any immediate return, alongside beginning a formal search for a new chief executive. Arm boss Rene Haas had been widely seen as a front-runner for the role.

Tech chiefs rallied round

But an online petition which attracted hundreds of thousands of signatories including from the likes of Tesla boss Elon Musk, alongside Trump’s intervention and a public plea from Huang for a quick reinstatement, appear to have tilted the odds back in his favour.

Huang’s shock return to Nvidia, which echoed a similar move to bring Sam Altman back to run Open AI in 2024, are likely to cement the dominance over the company by the firm’s co-founder for the foreseeable future, raising questions over standards of corporate governance in the world’s biggest tech businesses.

The move “shows everything rotten in Silicon Valley’s leadership and culture,” former Mark Zuckerberg adviser, Dex Hunter-Torricke, said. “Lying to the board should be a dealbreaker for any board, but normal rules don’t apply.”

articles.title: As it happened: FTSE 100 falls as AI fears resume after Huang comeback rally
articles.summary:
Welcome back to City AM‘s FTSE 100 liveblog.

Stocks fell on Tuesday after the ecstatic rally prompted by Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia chief executive faded fast. US indexes had soared to recent highs following the news but reversed in the afternoon, as the FTSE 100 also trailed in the red.
