articles.title: Expanded voucher program to help sustain private schools — COCOPEA
articles.summary:
MANILA, Philippines – The newly passed law that expanded the voucher program for poor students in private K to 12 schools is seen to help sustain operations of private institutions amid declining enrollment and economic pressures, the Coordinating Council of Private Educational Associations (COCOPEA) said on Tuesday, November 24. 

Republic Act (RA) No. 12327 or the Basic Education Voucher Assistance Act broadened the Expanded Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education (E-GASTPE) Act to include kindergarten and elementary school.

Currently, the decades-old E-GASTPE Act only provides tuition aid to students in private junior and senior high schools.

COCOPEA chairperson Irineo Alvaro Jr. said the reform would help decongest public schools, and affirms the inherent right and responsibility of parents to choose the best education setting for their children. 

“By subsidizing a significant portion of tuition in recognized private schools, the government can alleviate financial burdens on families,” Alvaro said in a press conference. 

“The voucher program is a real game changer in re-centering our education policy around the Filipino family, not just decongestion.”

Must Read

Voucher program now covers kinder to Grade 12 under new law

Alvaro noted that enrollment rates in private schools, particularly small institutions, declined by 6% to 10% compared to last year, as they cannot match subsidized institutions and the level of teachers’ salary in public schools. Some have already closed this year, he added, without providing further details.

“We really need to sustain our existence despite all of these. And this RA 12327 is a good start. I hope this is a work in progress that could extend up to the tertiary [level],” Alvaro said.

To prevent “ghost students,” COCOPEA said it is coordinating with the Department of Education (DepEd) in pushing transparency for all transactions.

The group will also collaborate with the DepEd as the agency crafts the implementing rules and regulations of the new law.

COCOPEA legal counsel Joseph Noel Estrada wants a stronger role for the Private Education Assistance Committee (PEAC), which is the co-implementer of the tuition aid for junior high and senior high school students.

The new law does not mention PEAC, but it mandates the creation of the Bureau of Private Education under the DepEd.

“We will continue to help PEAC and explore systems to ensure that there will be no leakage, no corruption, no anomalies and irregularities,” Estrada said.

‘Stagflation’ among considerations for tuition hike 

COCOPEA also called for urgent action to help schools survive economic pressures. 

“Like every Filipino household, private educational institutions are hit hard by rising inflation, surging electricity and operating costs, and frequent calamities. These pressures threaten the survival of many schools and make life harder for their students, faculty, and staff,” Alvaro said.

He said sustainability of private schools would be ensured if there are policy changes promoting freedom to use flexible learning and training setups, fair and timely tuition adjustments, prompt release of government subsidies, less red tape, and respect for academic freedom.

Particularly, COCOPEA is pushing for a review of existing tuition policies so that private institutions can sustain fair compensation and support for faculty, invest in modern facilities, and continuously improve the quality of instruction. 

Father Karel San Juan, president of Ateneo de Davao University and the Catholic Educational Association of the Philippines, said private schools are “very sensitive” to economic forecasts as they are tuition-dependent.

“The inflation rate in the Philippines is really escalating…the economists are projecting stagflation in the Philippines. [At the] macro level, we’re considering that. At the micro level, in our respective cities, towns where we operate all over the country, we’re considering local inflation as well,” San Juan said in the same press conference. 

Stagflation refers to the combination of weak economic growth and high inflation.

Must Read

[In This Economy] The Philippines has entered stagflation territory

Other considerations cited by COCOPEA were climate disruptions, including the impact of El Niño, adjustments in minimum wage, and competition.

San Juan said consultations with parents, students, and faculty must also be done before proposing tuition increases. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Playwright, filmmaker Dustin Celestino inducted into Palanca Hall of Fame
articles.summary:
MANILA, Philippines – Multi-awarded Filipino playwright and filmmaker Dustin Edward Celestino — whose work has been recognized across theater, film, and literature — was inducted into the Hall of Fame of the Carlos Palanca Memorial Awards for Literature on Tuesday, November 24, in Makati City.

Celestino’s full-length Filipino play, Kritisismo, earned him his fifth first-place honor, solidifying his place in the prestigious Hall of Fame of the Palanca Awards, widely regarded as the local equivalent of the Pulitzer Prize.

“It’s such an honor to be included among writers I have the greatest respect for. I’m also very happy to be part of a club that includes good friends and writing peers Mikael Co, Guelan Luarca, and Joshua So,” Celestino told Rappler. All three became Hall of Famers in 2024.

Elmer Gatchalian, a member of the board of judges for Dulang Ganap na Haba (Filipino Division), said, “We were all impressed by Kritisismo because of its dramatic structure and metatheatrical form. The full-length play stands out for its intellectual depth and sharp dialogue that examines power, class divide, and systemic oppression.”

Celestino’s other entry, Seen, won second place in the Full-Length Play category, English Division, this year.

Since 2017, Celestino has received four other Palanca first-prize awards in the full-length play category:

Fidelity (English), 2025

Ang Duyan ng Magiting (The Cradle of the Brave) (Filipino), 2019

The Story of This Father (English), 2017

Ang Pangahas na si Pepe Rodriguez (The Malevolent Pepe Rodriguez) (Filipino), 2017

His other Palanca wins include second prize for the full-length English play Birdie in 2024; second prize for the one-act Filipino play Elehiya in 2025; third prize for the full-length English play The Lost Filipino Patriots of America in 2022; third prize for the one-act Filipino play Fermata in 2023; and third prize for the full-length Filipino play A.Ni.Mal in 2025.

The Palanca Awards is the longest-running and most prestigious literary competition in the country. Established in 1950 and named after philanthropist and businessman Don Carlos Palanca Sr., it is sponsored by the Carlos Palanca Foundation, Inc., and is considered the gold standard in Philippine writing excellence.

Screenwriter

In 2026, Celestino won Indie Movie Screenwriter of the Year at the 42nd PMPC Star Awards for Movies for Habang Nilalamon ng Hydra ang Kasaysayan (As Hydra Devours History). He was also nominated for Best Original Screenplay at the Luna Awards and Best Screenplay at The Eddys.

Celestino’s films Habang Nilalamon ng Hydra ang Kasaysayan and A.Ni.Mál were both nominated for Best Film at the Cinemalaya Independent Film Festival in 2025 and 2026, respectively.

In 2023, Ang Duyan ng Magiting won the Special Jury Prize at Cinemalaya, earned seven Gawad Urian nominations including Best Picture, and was one of seven films shortlisted as the Philippines’ official entry to the 96th Academy Awards.

Strange Frequencies: Taiwan Killer Hospital, which he co-wrote, competed at the 2024 Metro Manila Film Festival.

Meanwhile, Utopia won the Special Jury Prize at the 2019 Cinema One Originals Film Festival and earned Celestino nominations for Best Director and Best Screenplay.

Over seven years, Celestino staged four one-act plays at the Cultural Center of the Philippines’ Virgin Labfest (VLF): Mga Eksena sa Buhay ng Kontrabida (Scenes from the Life of an Antagonist), Doggy, Ang Munting Liwanag sa Madilim na Sulok ng Isang Serbeserya sa Maynila (The Glimmer of Light in a Dark Corner of a Beerhouse in Manila), and Fermata.

The VLF also “opened more doors” for Celestino. Those doors included writing for the series Unconditional (later streamed on Netflix) and the Viva series Di Na Muli on TV5.

Video rental shop

Celestino was born in 1983 as the eldest of four children —  three boys and a girl — to entrepreneur Edgardo Celestino and teacher and preschool owner Rocelyn Domingo.

Only English books lined their bookshelves while growing up in a two-bedroom bungalow in Quezon City, making English his first language.

“I couldn’t write in Filipino well until I was in college,” he said.

Celestino’s father — who also worked as a sales representative for pharmaceutical company Unilab — owned a chain of video rental shops, and Dustin helped curate the titles they acquired.

“I watched movies as a kid, because we had video shops. At age 11 or 12, I was already asked to curate our video shop’s library because I loved watching movies,” he recalled.

Name it — Betamax, VHS, 4+1 rental promos — he watched them all and read the covers of the VHS tapes. His father favored action flicks starring Bruce Willis, Sylvester Stallone, and Mark Dacascos, while Dustin was drawn to horror.

Celestino initially took Film at De La Salle University in Manila before shifting to Philosophy with a minor in Translation. He was part of the Malate Literary Folio from 2000 to 2004.

He began joining writing competitions in 2003 and 2004, winning four times.

“I was initially into writing English fiction,” he said. It’s a path that led him to writers’ workshops organized by Iyas, Ateneo de Manila University, and Silliman University in Dumaguete.

Mythology

Celestino loved Greek mythology as a child. Aside from watching Jason and the Argonauts on Channel 9 — which “started my initial interest in mythology” — the idea of using myths as metaphors for contemporary struggles came from The Myth of Sisyphus by French philosopher and novelist Albert Camus.

What appealed to him most were the stories of mortals because they were “more relatable: Pygmalion, Icarus, Orpheus, Cassandra.”

Among his favorite foreign authors are European existentialists Camus, French philosopher and playwright Jean-Paul Sartre, and Russian novelist Fyodor Dostoevsky.

He also admires Russian-American novelist Vladimir Nabokov, Czech-French novelist Milan Kundera, Czech writer Franz Kafka, German-Swiss poet and novelist Hermann Hesse, German novelist and poet Günter Grass, and American fictionists Philip Roth and Ernest Hemingway.

“They were very good with narratives,” he said.

Among Filipino writers, the one Celestino deems closest to them is Gregorio Brillantes.

“I think Gregorio Brillantes was the best Filipino writer,” Celestino said.

Teacher

Celestino has always been a teacher, just like his mother. As a speed reader, he easily handled one of the hardest parts of the job: grading papers. 

He began teaching high school at St. Scholastica’s College. Later, while he was teaching college freshmen and sophomores at Asia Pacific College, the Philippines’ shift to the K-12 curriculum left him without work in the mid-2010s.

“Walang mabigay na workload sa akin (No workload could be given to me). I was demoralized. I had to take on another job,” he shared.

He was grateful for a role as creative director, where he also handled corporate social responsibility, at an internal communications company owned by a La Salle batchmate, though he struggled with the daily commute from Fairview.

He eventually resigned to focus on writing. He devoted the first 100 days of 2017 to studying playwriting formats and reading past Palanca winners.

“I had nine entries that year,” he recalled. Both of his full-length plays (in Filipino and English) won first prize.

“I had a knack for writing screenplays,” he said. “I started writing more.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: PM says Seoul's development aid will focus on helping partner nations grow on their own
articles.summary: Korea will focus its official development assistance (ODA) on helping recipient nations tackle problems on their own and grow, Prime Minister Han Seong-sook said Wednesday. Han made the remark during a ceremony commemorating International Development Cooperation Day that marks South Korea's accession in 2009 to the OECD Development Assistance Committee, the first case of a recipient nation joining the grouping of rich countries. "The number of places in need of assistance continues to grow due to conflicts, climate disasters, famine and diseases while at the same time, the financial resources remain limited, leaving us with the task of how to maximize the impact of our support," Han said. "For us to address this together, partner nations must develop the capacity to solve their own problems and grow," she said. As an example, Han cited the case of the Korea International Cooperation Agency providing support for 12 startups in Indonesia over the past five years, with $1 million worth of grants given to them leading to $50 million in private investment. articles.title: Remains of Korean Army corporal killed in Vietnam War to be returned home
articles.summary: The remains of a Korean soldier who died while serving in the Vietnam War will return home, marking the repatriation 59 years after his death, the defense ministry said Wednesday. The ceremony marking the return of late Army Cpl. Ahn Gyu-tae will take place at Seoul Airport in Seongnam, south of Seoul, overseen by Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul, according to the ministry. His remains will be transferred home from Hawaii via the Air Force's C-130 aircraft, it added. Ahn, who served as an Army corporal under the 9th Infantry Division, was deployed to Vietnam in August 1966 in the midst of the war between communist-backed North Vietnam and the United States and its allies, including South Vietnam and Korea. There, he took part in several military operations before he died from a critical gunshot wound that he sustained during a search mission in 1967. He was 23 at the time. His remains were supposed to be returned home via a U.S. transport aircraft, but the plan fell apart as the plane crashed while evading enemy attack on its way to a local airport. articles.title: Father Ham Je-doe, who made more than 60 trips to North Korea, dead at 93
articles.summary: CHEONGJU — Father Ham Je-doe, born Gerard Hammond, an American Maryknoll missionary who spent more than six decades in Korea and devoted himself to humanitarian work in North Korea, died Monday. He was 93. The Diocese of Cheongju announced that Father Hammond, who had been hospitalized at Cheongju St. Mary's Hospital due to age-related illness, died at 7:46 a.m. Monday. Born in Philadelphia in 1933, Hammond graduated from Maryknoll Seminary and was ordained a priest before choosing Korea as his first mission destination in 1960. After arriving in Korea, he served as director of the Sacred Heart Orphanage in Cheongju, North Chungcheong Province, caring for children. He later spent more than 30 years conducting pastoral work in the Diocese of Cheongju, dedicating himself to evangelization and social service in the region. In particular, while serving as the first pastor of Sudong Catholic Church in Cheongju, he donated an inheritance from his grandparents to secure land for a church and kindergarten. articles.title: Changwon court judges to discuss judicial independence
articles.summary: Judges at a district court in the southeastern city of Changwon are set to meet Wednesday to discuss judicial independence amid the ruling Democratic Party of Korea's (DPK) push to impeach Supreme Court Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae, legal sources said. The regular general meeting of all judges at the Changwon District Court was scheduled to take place in the afternoon, with independence of the judiciary on the agenda, according to the sources. The session comes after the DPK said last week it will seek Cho's impeachment, accusing the top court of failing to properly respond to former President Yoon Suk Yeol's botched 2024 martial law bid among other reasons. Some judges across the nation have voiced criticism against the DPK's move. Kang Dong-won, a senior judge at the Seoul Family Court who also chairs the national conference of judge representatives, accused the DPK of "going beyond the bounds" in a post Sunday on the court's internal network.

HILS and HIAR are affiliated with the university. Under the agreement, the three institutions will jointly develop and offer courses, lectures, workshops and practical programs in mediation and negotiation. They also plan to conduct collaborative research, organize seminars and academic events, and provide students with domestic and international internship opportunities. articles.title: Korea slashes nationality reinstatement wait times to 9 months for ethnic Koreans living abroad
articles.summary: The Ministry of Justice has significantly accelerated the nationality reinstatement process for ethnic Koreans living abroad, cutting the average review time by four months — from 13 months down to nine. For applicants experiencing the fastest processing, wait times have been reduced by as much as seven months, offering swift relief to thousands eager to formally reconnect with their homeland. The breakthrough stems from an intensive, three-month processing campaign conducted between August and October, according to the ministry. Facing a growing backlog fueled by a steady rise in applications from ethnic Koreans living abroad, the ministry overhauled its operational capacity. Previously, a single dedicated officer handled the workload, processing an average of roughly 220 cases per month. By deploying four additional specialists to the team, the ministry dramatically scaled up its output, resolving a total of 4,664 cases over the three-month period. articles.title: Late firefighter in Bucheon factory blaze named person of national merit
articles.summary: A firefighter killed in the line of duty while battling a factory fire in a city southwest of Seoul last month has been registered as a person of national merit, the veterans ministry said Wednesday. The decision was finalized upon approval by a review committee of the Ministry of Patriots and Veterans Affairs on Friday and his bereaved family was notified earlier this week, according to the ministry. Fire Lt. Kim Jin-seok died from severe injuries sustained while battling a blaze that broke out at a metalworking factory in Bucheon, just west of Seoul, on Oct. 16. Six other firefighters were also injured. Kim's death sparked calls for a review of firefighting protocols amid questions over whether crews should be rushed into containment efforts without properly assessing the scene to minimize on-site risks to personnel. Local authorities have since launched a probe into the incident to determine whether safety protocols were adequately followed. articles.title: Seoul Metro labor, management reach last-minute deal to avoid strike
articles.summary: Labor and management at Seoul Metro reached a last-minute agreement on wages and working conditions Wednesday, avoiding a planned general strike that could have disrupted the morning commute, according to labor and management representatives. All three labor unions at Seoul Metro, which operates subway Lines 1-8 and part of Line 9, reached agreements with management and called off their planned general strike, which had been scheduled to begin with the first trains of the day. The two sides agreed to cap wage increases at 3.5 percent, while management will put on hold its existing restructuring plan to eliminate 2,212 jobs and hire 500 new employees Union 1, 2 and 3 have 9,100, 2,560 and 2,220 members, respectively. With the government setting a 3.5 percent guideline for increases in total labor costs at public institutions, wages were not a major point of contention between labor and management. articles.title: From local comfort food to global franchise: Chinese malatang king's Korea test
articles.summary: At around 7 p.m. on a recent Monday, more than half of the dozen or so tables were occupied at a Yangguofu Malatang restaurant in Yeoksam, an office-packed area in Seoul's Gangnam District. Vegetables, fish balls, rice cakes and instant noodles lined a refrigerated self-service topping bar, while pickled radish, peanuts and dipping sauces were available nearby. Two employees juggled cooking, payments, serving and clearing tables in the orange-hued restaurant. Yangguofu Group, one of China's largest malatang chains with nearly 7,000 outlets worldwide, has grown its overseas network from just over 20 in early 2023 to more than 200 across 30 countries and territories, as it steps up its global expansion. Yet the company is a much smaller player in Korea, where malatang — which literally translates to “numbing, spicy, scalding-hot” — found a receptive audience in a country fond of spicy food and hot soups. articles.title: As AI cheating fears soar, does college matter that much in Korea?
articles.summary: As someone who never took the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), I found myself asking a question last week while covering anxiety over cheating with artificial intelligence (AI) — a concern that rocked Korea. “Is college really that important in Korea?” My answer is yes. Korean society does push people hard to go to college — and not just any college but a good one. When I was a high school senior, I decided to travel around the world instead of going to college. After a year of working as a cleaner in Australia to fund the trip, I spent another year touring 24 countries. Over the course of those two years, one of the most common refrains from fellow Koreans I met on the road was, “You have to go to college.” True to that advice, Koreans go to college at one of the highest rates in the world. Forty-year-old Zeeshan Ali became the first Pakistani astronaut to enter orbit on Wednesday, after China’s Shenzhou-24 spacecraft entered its preset orbit following liftoff from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre.

A Long March 2-F rocket was used for the launch. It took off in a cloud of flames and smoke at 8:18am Beijing Time (5:18am Pakistan Time) under a pink sky, video from state broadcaster CCTV showed.

A send-off ceremony was held for three astronauts who make up the mission’s crew at the launch centre before they entered the spacecraft capsule.

The spacecraft successfully separated from the carrier rocket roughly 10 minutes after blast-off and entered into orbit, the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) said.

“The spacecraft is functioning well. I declare the Shenzhou-24 launch mission a complete success,” an official at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre announced.

Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, who is in China, witnessed the send-off and the mission’s launch.

Later, he posted on X: “As Shenzhou-24 lifts off this morning, Nov 25, carrying Zeeshan Ali, Pakistan’s first astronaut, a new era begins for Pakistan’s space programme. With him, the Pakistani flag rises into orbit, lifting the hopes and aspirations of 260 million Pakistanis for technological advancement and space exploration. From highways to information super highways to skyways, Pakistan-China friendship and CPEC rises higher than the skies.

“This is Pakistan’s URAAN (flight) into space, and it is only the beginning of a brighter and more glorious future.”

The Shenzhou-24 spacecraft is bound for China’s Tiangong space station, and when the spacecraft docks with it, Ali will also become the first foreign national to board it.

China’s Tang Hongbo is commanding the mission, with Wu Yi serving as mission pilot and Ali as payload specialist.

Ali is expected to spend around a week in space, conducting various experiments alongside the Chinese crew. Pakistan’s space agency, Suparco, said Ali would conduct experiments in orbit, including cultivating microalgae as a potential food and oxygen source for future space missions, and testing the effects of spaceflight on quinoa seeds.

Meanwhile, the CMSA said the crew will conduct around 90 experiments during the mission.

The agency said the mission’s objectives included conducting an orbital rotation with the crew of the earlier Shenzhou-23 mission, carrying out routine operations and maintenance of the space station, and continuing space science research, including experiments involving space payloads.

‘Carrying hopes of 250m Pakistanis’

Earlier in April, Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud were chosen from Pakistan to start training in China. Pakistan’s space agency Suparco and CMSA signed a cooperation agreement in February 2025, under which two Pakistanis were to train in China, with one joining a mission on the Tiangong space station operated by Beijing.

Eventually, Ali was chosen to join the Chinese mission.

Speaking at a press briefing in Jiayuguan on Tuesday, Ali said he was “deeply grateful” to the Chinese government for helping “us realise our dream of going into space”.

He said he arrived at the Astronaut Centre of China a few months ago, carrying with him the hopes of 250 million Pakistani people.

Ali said he believed that “what comes after this flight matters more than the flight itself”.

“This mission is not a finish line; it is a launch pad. And I hope the next chapter of China-Pakistan space cooperation will grow from one astronaut, one flight to multiple joint flights, to the Moon, Mars and beyond.”

Addressing Pakistanis, he said: “I now feel the true weight of the words of our Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, when he told me that we were about to write a new chapter in Pakistan’s history. I want to assure you that I am not flying for myself. I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulders, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis.

“To every child who is watching while I am in orbit, just look up at the sky and remember that I am up there with your dreams.”

In his message to his family, he said: “I want to say that I will travel farther from home than ever before. But I promise you one thing: whenever I look back at the Earth for the first time, I will always search for the light of our home before I look at anything else. No matter how far I fly, we will still share the same Moon, and I will still be looking back at the same Earth.”

Stay at Tiangong

China’s self-built station, named Tiangong or Celestial Palace in Chinese, has been fully operational since late 2022. It can host up to six astronauts during handovers when an arriving three-person crew overlaps with the departing crew.

This time, the handover will be different.

Shenzhou-23 commander Zhu Yangzhu ​will stay on to support Beijing’s study ​of how the human body copes ⁠in space — a crucial step towards a planned crewed mission to the moon and a potential journey to Mars. The rest of the Shenzhou-23 crew will depart Tiangong alongside Ali.

Zhu, who will stay for a year, will hold the record for the longest single ​stay in orbit by a Chinese astronaut by the time he leaves.

Beijing has poured billions into China’s space programme as it aims to land astronauts on the Moon before 2030, a race in which the United States is also competing with its Artemis programme.

Additional input from Reuters and AFP

articles.title: Pakistan eyes $1.21 billion disbursement next month
articles.summary:
ISLAMABAD: The Exe­cutive Board of the Intern­a­tional Monetary Fund (IMF) is expected to appr­ove on Dec 11 the disbursement of about $1.21 billion to Pakistan under two concurrent program­mes — the $7bn Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and the $1.4bn Resilience and Sus­t­ainability Facility (RSF).

The approval would mark the completion of the fourth review under the EFF and the third under the RSF.

Upon approval, Pakis­tan will have access to about $1bn (760 million Special Drawing Rights, or SDRs) under the EFF and about $210m (154m SDRs) under the RSF, bringing total disbursements under the two arrangements to about $5.7bn.

The two sides had reac­hed a staff-level agr­eem­ent (SLA) in the first week of October. Both programmes — the 37-month EFF and the 28-month RSF — are scheduled to conclude by September 2027.

The IMF staff had acknowledged in the SLA that programme implementation under the EFF rema­ined broadly on track despite a challenging external environment.

It also noted Pakistan’s strong commitment to preserving macroeconomic stability, strengthening public finances, keeping inflation within the State Bank of Pakistan’s target range on a sustained basis, enhancing energy sector viability and strengthening social protection.

The IMF team, led by Iva Petrova, had also completed the 2026 Article IV consultation, a regular assessment of the country’s economic performance and policies, alongside the fourth review under the EFF and the third under the RSF during discussions held from Sept 23 to Oct 7.

The IMF staff had noted that, supported by the EFF, the authorities had successfully navigated the impact of the Middle East conflict and strong policies helped preserve macroeconomic stability.

Real GDP growth reached four per cent in the first three quarters of FY26. Although higher energy prices and supply disruptions subsequently weakened growth momentum somewhat, the IMF estimated full-year growth at 3.6pc.

The Fund had also noted that the current account remained broadly balanced in FY26, supported by strong remittances, while gross foreign exchange reserves rose to about $21.5bn by end-September.

Sovereign credit rating upgrades and renewed access to international financial markets also pointed to stronger policy credibility.

Nevertheless, the Fund highlighted considerable risks, particularly those arising from geopolitical tensions, volatile energy prices, tighter global financial conditions and trade disruptions.

The two sides had agreed that maintaining sound macroeconomic policies was critical to safeguarding stability amid continued vulnerability to external shocks.

In this regard, policy priorities would continue to include maintaining fiscal discipline through steadfast implementation of the FY27 budget, anchored by an underlying primary surplus of 2pc of GDP and supported by tax policy and revenue administration measures to place public debt on a sustainable downward trajectory.

Published in Dawn, November 25th, 2026

articles.title: What happens when a bank ducks rules in Pakistan? For Deutsche Bank, perhaps nothing
articles.summary:
In 2018, the world turned its microscope on Pakistan’s financial system. Placed on the Financial Action Task Force’s (FATF) “gray list”, the country was thrust into a frantic race to prove it could secure its financial system against the flow of illicit capital. It was a moment of national urgency, defined by rigorous audits and a desperate need to reclaim international legitimacy in a landscape shadowed by allegations of money laundering and terror financing.

The decision sent shockwaves through the country’s financial system and the resulting restrictions battered the economy.

Yet, even as policymakers were scrambling to bolster the defences of the nation’s financial system, vulnerabilities in the internal systems of Deutsche Bank’s Pakistan operations were complicating the fight against illicit money flows.

The global banking giant’s own assessment had classified Pakistan as a “restricted” high-risk country, subjecting businesses connected to it to additional checks and limitations. An internal report cited Pakistan’s “terrorism and Taliban links” and proximity to Iran as key reasons for the classification. Bank documents, however, show a history of overlooked alerts and bypassed regulations, and in some instances, an inability to identify who was truly moving the money in this “restricted country”.

These internal records are part of over 15 million internal Deutsche Bank files leaked to the journalists Josy Joseph and Khadija Sharife. The records span many of the bank’s most sensitive departments: financial crime, sanctions monitoring, internal auditing, and the units responsible for deciding whether risky clients stay or go. This report is part of Inside Deutsche Bank, a months-long investigation of the leak involving over 200 journalists from more than 50 countries.

The records reviewed by Dawn do not necessarily establish that suspicious or illicit transactions passed through the bank. What they reveal, however, is that while Pakistan was under intense international scrutiny over its financial controls, one of the world’s largest banks, while operating within the territory, struggled to distinguish customers from non-customers, monitor financial transactions and implement safeguards against financial crime.

The Pakistan operation

Deutsche Bank has held a commercial banking license in Pakistan since 1962. It processes hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of transactions into, out of and within the country every year. It currently employs close to 100 staff in its Karachi and Lahore branches, offering Pakistan-based clients a “wide range of corporate and investment bank products and services, including foreign exchange, fixed income sales and trading, cash management, trade finance and treasury solutions for corporates”.

Over the years, the bank’s internal controls against financial crime have been found wanting in multiple jurisdictions across the world. It has paid billions of dollars in fines and settlements over interest-rate manipulation, failures to prevent money laundering and other misconduct.

In Pakistan, however, its small yet significant operation has maintained an image of respectability, not once being named in any scandal or accused of involvement in financial irregularities.

According to internal documents, Pakistan has been one of the most active countries in Deutsche Bank’s global trade finance business. In 2016, it ranked third by the number of letters of credit handled by the bank, behind only China and India. That year, Deutsche Bank processed an estimated €872 million in incoming funds and €255 million in outgoing funds for Pakistan.

Across its global network, the bank exchanged around 187,000 incoming and 174,000 outgoing cross-border payment instructions involving Pakistan in the same period. About six in 10 were in US dollars.

Locally, the bank’s operations were relatively small and largely hands-on. An internal Deutsche Bank Pakistan spreadsheet dated December 2019 shows its local teams dealt with an average of about 4,560 items a day across cash counters, cheque clearing, payment orders and electronic payments. None of these was fully automated, according to the document.

The spreadsheet also recorded more than 14,000 daily reviews of transactions flagged by sanctions screening, illustrating the substantial compliance workload the bank faced alongside its routine operations.

Local compliance challenges

In October 2019, the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) introduced key requirements under its Trade-Based Money Laundering (TBML) framework and ordered banks to implement them with immediate effect. However, after feedback from some banks on implementation challenges, the regulator extended the deadline to September 30, 2020.

The framework, seen by Dawn, came on the heels of pressure from the FATF and aimed to strengthen “trade-related Anti-Money Laundering/Combating Financing of Terrorism (AML/CFT) regime and restrict possible misuse of banking channels”. It was part of a broader overhaul of processes relating to financial institutions.

Yet, internal records show Deutsche Bank Pakistan failed to implement two essential safeguards months after the September 2020 deadline: a price due diligence mechanism to identify artificially inflated or undervalued trade transactions; and an automated Management Information System (MIS) to monitor suspicious activity across its vast transaction volume.

“DB Pakistan Trade Finance has not fulfilled the SBP’s Trade Based Money Laundering (TBML) Framework requirements on implementation of a price due diligence mechanism and an automated MIS tool,” Khurram Amanullah, the bank’s principal auditor for Pakistan, wrote in an email on July 30, 2021, almost 10 months after the SBP’s revised deadline.

The email was addressed to Markus Weick, who was part of the bank’s Trade Finance Product Management team in Germany. At least a dozen other bank staff were copied.

According to Amanullah, “DB Pakistan Trade Finance spent excessive time in deciding whether to implement the relevant system in-house or outsourced to external vendor. (Lack of Diligence).”

Amanullah and Weick did not respond to requests for comment.

This wasn’t the first time the bank had flagged shortcomings in its trade finance processes in Pakistan. An earlier group audit, published in 2017, into Deutsche Bank Pakistan’s operations in 2016 had flagged similar concerns, stating: “Trade Finance Operations (TFO) does not always check whether underlying goods (HS Codes) for letter of credit (LC) transactions meet local requirements. In addition, Trade Product Management do not fully document expected client trade flows required to monitor [anti-money laundering] risk and identify potential red flags (GTB Due Diligence policy requirement).”

This was almost three years before the SBP ordered banks to address such risks. Yet it seems nothing had been done to mitigate them even by July 2021.

Whose money? Who knows

Beyond trade finance protocols, the 2017 audit report flagged another discovery: “DB Pakistan does not perform transaction filtering (sanction screening) for manual domestic cheque payments (€4.6bn in 2016) and a subset of local bank payments made through DBDC (global app).”

All banks in Pakistan are required to cross-check their clients against sanctions lists — such as the United Nations Security Council Consolidated Sanctions List and the National Counter Terrorism Authority Proscribed Persons List — and report any irregularities to the Financial Monitoring Unit, Pakistan’s central financial intelligence unit.

A banker with over two decades of experience in the compliance departments of various Pakistani banks told Dawn that the SBP requires banks to screen all active clients against these lists every month. “The lists are frequently updated, sometimes even within hours, so it’s common practice to perform the screening regularly,” he explained.

The 2017 audit report identified the risk that “DB Pakistan may process transactions with sanctioned/embargo counterparties or jurisdictions without detection.” The bank was clearly wary that some suspicious transactions may have escaped detection, especially considering the number of transactions and the quantum of funds involved.

This was against the Deutsche Bank Group’s own Embargo Policy, which mandates that “all transactions resulting in the transfer of assets or which instruct the transfer of assets are to be filtered against the applicable embargo lists prior to leaving DB Group, or subject to further processing within DB Group, to ensure DB Group does not process transactions with sanctioned designations”.

In 2016, the report noted, the matter had been escalated by the Pakistan operations staff to senior management, but the former were advised ”not to do anything further” because “… a system flag was due to be implemented across the group”.

This wasn’t the first time the bank had faced such a situation in the region. In 2015, according to the audit report, Deutsche Bank had paid a $258 million fine “as a result of sanction breaches for transactions in embargoed Middle East territories”. The report detailed that Deutsche Bank Pakistan had processed 76,821 unfiltered cheques worth €4.6 billion — €3.5 billion in deposits and €1.1 billion in payments — in 2016 alone. “The majority (circa €2.9bn of deposits) relates to one high-risk client, which is in the process of being off-boarded,” said the report. The audit report was silent on who this high-risk client was and why they were being off-boarded.

Another audit report from 2020 on Deutsche Bank Pakistan’s anti-financial crime functions noted that not a single Suspicious Activity Report or Suspicious Transaction Report was generated by the bank between July 2019 and June 2020 — a highly unusual occurrence given the volume of transactions the bank was handling. Banks must file such reports to legal and regulatory authorities whenever their internal compliance checks detect potential money laundering, terror financing or other financial crime.

Confusion over KYC function

In September 2019, Chiara Monaco from the anti-financial crime unit at Deutsche Bank’s headquarters in Frankfurt emailed bank staff in Pakistan to flag a concern regarding “certain sub-accounts in Pakistan belonging to customers not KYC’ed”.

KYC stands for “Know Your Customer” or “Know Your Client”. This is the information-gathering process by which a bank checks who you are, works out what you use your account for, and decides how risky you are as a customer. Banks need it to meet anti-money laundering (AML) and Combating the Financing of Terrorism (CFT) rules.

In another email the next day, Monaco wrote: “We found 1000s of subaccounts in Pakistan without KYC, opened for custody purposes and belonging to clients of State Street Bank and Bank of NY Mellon.”

“Can you please help [us] to fully understand the business model, the setup and background behind these accounts. They have not been KYC’ed,” she added.

The emails triggered a debate among the bank’s personnel regarding the nature of these accounts and whether they were subject to KYC regulations. Custody is a banking service where a bank holds and protects financial assets — stocks, bonds, securities and the like — on behalf of clients. In this instance, the “sub-accounts” referred to Special Convertible Rupee Accounts (SCRA) maintained by Deutsche Bank Pakistan for two major international financial institutions, both based in the United States.

An SCRA account, introduced by the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) in 2008, is a kind of specialised, repatriable bank account that allows non-resident investors, foreign nationals and overseas Pakistanis to trade freely in local capital markets.

The sub-accounts in question held money in the form of securities or treasury bonds belonging to other investors, many of whom never dealt with Deutsche Bank or its Pakistan operations directly.

“The local AML/CFT Regulations of State Bank of Pakistan require due diligence/KYC to be performed on the customers’ of the bank, where such underlying accounts do not fall under the definition of customers as per the regulations,” Zeeshan Waheed, the head of the compliance and anti-financial crime unit in Pakistan, wrote back. He added, “very recently we had a review being conducted by the Central Bank’s Inspection team and they had gone through the business model of DB Pakistan for Security Services and its operations, where they had not highlighted any concern/observation from an ML/TF risk point of view or overall controls with respect to compliance of local AML/CFT Regulations”.

A year earlier, the SBP had issued an update to its AML/CFT Regulations explicitly defining a “customer” as “any person having a relationship with the bank, such as holding deposits, placing money with the bank/DFI, availing financial services, locker facilities, safe deposit facilities, or custodial services”.

Under these regulations (Paras 7-9), banks are required to apply customer due diligence measures for all customers, including “identifying and verifying beneficial owners through reliable sources; understanding ownership/control structures for legal persons; and verifying senior managing officials where no controlling owner is identified”.

Moreover, according to the Anti-Money Laundering Act, 2010, a beneficial owner is defined as a “natural person who ultimately owns or controls a customer or the natural person on whose behalf a transaction is being conducted”.

The same law also provides a framework for due diligence as follows:

identify the customer and verify the customer’s identity on the basis of documents, data or information obtained from reliable and independent sources;

identify the beneficial owner and take reasonable measures to verify the beneficial owner’s identity on the basis of documents, data or information obtained from reliable sources and be satisfied that it knows who the beneficial owner is;

understand and, as appropriate, obtain information on the purpose and intended nature of the business relationship; and

monitor the business relationship on an ongoing basis.

Dawn reached out to Monaco and Waheed for comment, but did not hear back. Three bankers, who spoke to Dawn on condition of anonymity, said that the SBP requires banks to conduct customer due diligence (CDD) in these cases. “KYC/CDD requirements apply, although the precise extent of due diligence on each underlying investor depends on the account structure, customer relationship and applicable regulatory requirements,” one banker with over two decades of experience in compliance explained to Dawn via email. “Under Regulation R-2 of the SBP AML/CFT/CPF Regulations, banks must conduct CDD in accordance with the Anti-Money Laundering Act, 2010.”

Deutsche Bank Pakistan, the emails show, vacillated on whether the beneficiaries of custodial accounts were in fact its customers, despite the fact that the SBP and other banks did apply KYC requirements to such accounts.

The debate lasted more than two months before the issue was closed.

As of last year, Deutsche Bank Pakistan held Rs 143.63 billion in government securities and shares, as per its published financial statement. According to the statement, the bank does not treat these as its own assets. Until 2019 at least, it apparently did not know who the actual owners of these assets were.

The documents reviewed by Dawn do not make clear if the 2019 Trade-Based Money Laundering compliance framework and KYC disputes were ultimately resolved, whether any corrective measures addressed the concerns raised by senior compliance officials, or whether the deficiencies identified by auditors in 2021 were ever fully remedied.

Each of the audit reports reviewed by Dawn recommended short-term and long-term measures to be adopted by Deutsche Bank Pakistan to mitigate the risks flagged. It remains unclear whether these were implemented.

It also remains unclear whether any of these issues were taken up by the SBP as part of its annual audits. Despite repeated reminders, the SBP did not respond to a detailed questionnaire sent by Dawn.

In a summary response to over a dozen questions from Dawn, Deutsche Bank stated: “We do not comment on potential, former or existing client relationships.

“Deutsche Bank takes its obligations to prevent financial crime seriously and maintains controls designed to comply with applicable anti-money laundering, sanctions and other regulatory requirements.”

Editing by Roman Gautam/Himal Southasian; Header art by Mohsin Alam/Dawn

The Inside Deutsche Bank investigation was coordinated by Barracuda Media in South Africa, with technical support from the Data and Research Center (DARC) in Germany.

articles.title: Pakistan Customs seizes nearly 1kg of 'Multan-bound' marijuana in Karachi
articles.summary:
The Collectorate of Customs (CoC) (airports) in Karachi foiled a narcotics smuggling attempt and seized 900 grams of marijuana during routine scanning at the International Mail Office (IMO), Pakistan Customs said on Tuesday.

During routine scanning, Customs staff intercepted a “suspicious parcel” originating from Canada’s Ontario and destined for Multan, the statement said.

“The parcel was declared as ‘Books (Gift)’. However, physical examination by Preventive Officer Muhammad Shah Jahan revealed boxes of chocolates and cereals, within which the 900 grams of marijuana was concealed,” the press release said.

The seized marijuana was valued at approximately Rs27.25 million, Pakistan Customs said.

The consignment was shifted to the Directorate of Enforcement and Compliance (DEC) headquarters at Jinnah International Airport for further necessary proceedings.

A first information report (FIR) has been registered in the case and further legal proceedings were underway, Pakistan Customs said.

“Reflecting continued vigilance, Pakistan Customs remains committed to curbing narcotics smuggling and safeguarding public welfare.”

In July, Pakistan Customs seized 12kg of marijuana during routine scanning of a shipment originating from Bangkok at the International Mail Office in Karachi.

In August, a special court for the Control of Narcotic Substances (CNS) has sentenced three men to life in prison for attempting to traffic over 1.3 tonnes of charas to an African country.

articles.title: Cabinet approves deregulation of sugar sector to meet vital IMF benchmark
articles.summary:
ISLAMABAD: To meet a long-postponed structural benchmark of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the federal cabinet on Tuesday approved the deregulation of the sugar sector, an end to its export subsidies and free movement among the provinces.

The cabinet approved the ‘National Policy for Deregulation of Sugar Sector’ through circulation while Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif “recused himself from the sugar sector related decisions” owing to his immediate family’s sugar business, informed sources told Dawn.

The decision came after the government allowed the export of more than 400,000 tonnes of sugar on Friday, in addition to 200,000 tonnes already exported a few months ago.

The IMF has continuously pushed for a policy ending the government’s role in sugar sector operations, from sugarcane crop prices to sugar production and import-export, leaving it to market forces. The fund also minutely remained engaged with the terms and conditions of a ministerial committee which finalised the sugar deregulation policy.

Pakistan has been in breach of the structural benchmark of the IMF since June 2026 and its approval was mandatory for scheduling the IMF executive board meeting, now set for Dec 11.

The policy approval was hampered by Sindh’s virtual veto, although three other provinces had already consented to the draft. After hectic backdoor negotiations, the Sindh government finally cleared the policy on Nov 21 after securing certain amendments.

The policy was finalised by a ministerial committee led by Power Minister Awais Leghari. The committee also includes the ministers for finance, food security and economic affairs; the premier’s adviser for industries; the chairman of the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR); secretaries of concerned ministries and provincial chief secretaries, as well as other stakeholders.

Being a structural benchmark of the IMF, the timeline for the completion of the process was June 30, 2026. The fund proposed revised Terms of Reference (ToRs) on July 31, 2026 for incorporation in the ToRs of the committee, which were agreed to by the prime minister, official records seen by Dawn suggested.

The Ministry of Industries and Production, on the IMF’s directions, “inserted some amendments and shared the said draft policy with the IMF” by the end of August, which were fine-tuned by the fund again on Oct 1. It was insisted that the Sindh government’s agreement was necessary for completion of the structural benchmark.

The policy provides a predictable mechanism for imports and exports with a complete end to export subsidies, the cabinet was told. There will be no restrictions on the inter-provincial movement of sugar, and transitional arrangements have been provided for the current crushing season.

At the input stage, the government has removed restrictions on planting zones and cane varieties, providing freedom to cane producers to sell their crop to any buyer and mills to sell their product. The sugarcane price has now been left to market forces to determine, but there will be a negative list of banned sugar varieties.

At the processing stage, there will be no restriction on the establishment of new mills or capacity approvals for mills; the millers will have the freedom to choose raw material sources and take market-based production decisions. Price controls by the governments will come to an end.

For creating an enabling environment for smooth transition, the deregulation policy provides certain safeguards to the farmers in the shape of third-party validation of weighing scales, sucrose testing framework and interest payments by millers on the late payment of sugarcane dues.

The sugarcane cess has been promised for effective use of research, as well as easy access to credit for farmers and millers, along with farm mechanisation schemes going ahead.

The policy, nevertheless, retains the government’s right to maintain buffer sugar stocks and take measures to access correct and timely information on sugarcane crop, sugar production and market availability. It will also encourage working towards mandating ethanol blending and providing a fair and competitive market.

articles.title: 11 injured as Riyadh skyscraper hit second time in less than a week
articles.summary:
Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper was struck for the second time in days on Tuesday, injuring 11 people, as the coalition fighting Houthis denounced a “terrorist attack”.

The building, which was also attacked last Thursday, is one of several high-profile targets hit since hostilities with the Houthis restarted in July.

Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence reported Tuesday’s injuries and posted a picture of the landmark tower housing the headquarters of the Saudi Public Investment Fund (PIF).

The image showed some damage to the building about halfway up the facade, similar to the impact from a strike on the same tower on Nov 19, which caused damage but no injuries.

Reuters could not immediately determine when the image was taken or the extent of the further damage from the latest strike.

Saudi Civil Defence said the 11 people injured included two Saudi citizens, four Egyptian nationals, three Nepalese nationals and two Indian nationals.

“Relevant authorities responded to the incident immediately, implementing all established protocols and measures for handling such situations, and taking the necessary steps to ensure the safety of lives and property,” the Arabic statement said.

“One of the towers in the financial centre was targeted in a cowardly terrorist attack,” coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki said in a social media post, without naming the building.

Standing 385 metres high, the PIF tower is the most prominent landmark of King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD), a showcase for Saudi Arabia’s economic ambitions.

A witness told AFP that a vehicle fitted with a speaker had warned pedestrians in the area to take cover on Tuesday. No warning was sent to mobile phones about any threats to the capital.

Afterwards, police cars blocked some entrances to the gleaming financial district. With imposing skyscrapers, luxury shops and green spaces, the district also hosts the headquarters of the Saudi stock exchange along with multinationals such as Goldman Sachs.

An attack on the PIF is symbolic as the fund is driving efforts to diversify the oil-reliant Saudi economy — a project that has been complicated by the Middle East war and Houthi strikes.

A tower belonging to state oil giant Aramco in KAFD was hit earlier this month, while Riyadh’s international airport was repeatedly struck in October, with one attack killing 14 people.

The Houthis, who control much of western Yemen including the capital Sanaa, have been firing at Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and office buildings since Yemen’s frozen civil war reignited in July in a knock-on from the US-Iran war.

The attacks have caused the cancellation of most international flights to Riyadh, and forced Saudi Arabia to postpone or cancel major international events, including soccer’s AFC Asian Cup.

Such cowardly attacks undermine peace efforts: Pakistan

Pakistan strongly condemned the “terrorist attack carried out today by the Houthi militia”, the Foreign Office said.

In a statement, FO said Islamabad denounced “such cowardly attacks, which endanger civilians and civilian infrastructure, heighten regional tensions and undermine efforts to restore peace and stability”.

“Pakistan stands in full solidarity with Saudi Arabia in the face of these attacks. The Kingdom has every right to defend its territory and protect its citizens and residents,” FO affirmed.

It expressed Pakistan’s deep sympathies with those injured and their families and wished them swift and full recovery. FO also commended the Saudi authorities for their “prompt response” and the steps taken to protect lives and property.

Islamabad has condemned Houthi attacks repeatedly, including on international platforms, and termed them a grave violation of the kingdom’s sovereignty.

Pakistan and Riyadh have signed two defence pacts aimed at collective deterrence, the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement between the two and the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement that also includes Turkiye.

Under the Makkah Defence Alliance, Pakistani, Saudi and Turkish leaders met in Riyadh in October and agreed to deploy military forces and capabilities rapidly in the kingdom.

Pakistan is providing “whatever support is needed” to defend Saudi Arabia amid the Houthi attacks, the military’s spokesperson Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said later that month.

‘26 killed in Yemen attack’

On the ground in Yemen, the war has caused a major humanitarian crisis, with hundreds of thousands of people displaced from their homes since July.

The Houthis have seized swathes of territory, forcing forces aligned with the internationally recognised government to stage a major retreat this month.

The Saudi-led military coalition has been striking Houthi targets in the impoverished country.

On Tuesday, local officials said a coalition airstrike on buses and trucks killed 26 people in Lahj province. On the other hand, government forces blamed the Houthis for the attack.

As the conflict shows no sign of slowing, Britain sanctioned the Houthis and four of its top officials “for deliberately attempting to undermine stability” on Tuesday.

The measures include an asset freeze against the group and an asset freeze and travel ban on four figures, including security and intelligence head Abdul Hakim Hashem Ali al-Khaiwani, and interior affairs official Abdulkarim Amir al-Din Hussein al-Houthi.

The Saudi-led coalition intervened in Yemen in early 2015, after the Houthis had captured the capital Sanaa and sent the internationally recognised government fleeing to Aden.

The war left hundreds of thousands dead and triggered a humanitarian catastrophe before an uneasy ceasefire went into effect in 2022.

articles.title: Huang’s return fails to dispel doubts as Nvidia shares drop
articles.summary:
Technology shares led a market retreat on Tuesday as caution returned after Jensen Huang’s extraordinary return to AI giant Nvidia days after he was forced to resign, with investors bracing for further volatility in a key sector driving economic growth worldwide.

A day after Huang’s reinstatement as CEO drove Nvidia shares up more than 30 per cent, adding more than $900 billion to the firm’s market value, the euphoria dissipated as its stock lost almost 9pc mid-session.

Fellow tech behemoth and AI giant Anthropic also slumped, giving up around 12pc to $77.19, below its $83 price for last week’s IPO.

Monday aside, AI stocks had already sold off sharply throughout November on worries about profitability and the vast sums pumped into the sector.

Overall, the tech-heavy Nasdaq shed 2.3pc and the broader-based S&P 500 lost 1.1pc, while the Dow was just into the green around 1700 GMT (10pm PKT).

Europe’s main stock markets, which feature far fewer tech companies than their Asian and US rivals, finished a handful of percentage points lower after jumping on Monday in line with Wall Street.

Away from the tech sector, French pharmaceutical giant Sanofi revealed it would buy the US biopharma group Insmed, a specialist in respiratory treatments, for $41bn as it races to bulk up its development pipeline of new drugs.

Sanofi’s share price closed up almost 10pc following the news.

Huang had resigned less than two weeks ago over extramarital affairs, reportedly with an alleged Chinese spy as well as a senior Nvidia executive before US President Donald Trump noisily declared he should be brought back.

“Jensen’s return takes away one of the biggest unknowns hanging over the AI trade,” said Charu Chanana, an investment strategist at Saxo Markets.

“He is not just Nvidia’s CEO; he is arguably the biggest salesman for the entire AI ecosystem. His relationships with customers, suppliers and capital providers are difficult to replicate,” she said.

But “Jensen Huang alone cannot support the AI trade in the long term,” said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB.

“Nvidia’s stock price decline on Tuesday is to be expected after such a large rally in the previous session,” she added.

Analysts were in broad agreement that Huang’s return did not mean an end to probes or the uncertainty that has clouded the AI trade for six months.

The company remains under scrutiny from investigators including at the FBI and on Capitol Hill for allegedly helping Chinese firms gain access to Nvidia’s top-line chips.

Monday’s Wall Street surge had propelled Asian markets earlier on Tuesday, with Taipei surging 9pc higher as chip titans TSMC and MediaTek added nearly 10pc each.

Seoul piled on more than 6pc thanks to strong gains in fellow chip giants SK Hynix and Samsung, and Tokyo rose nearly 4pc, led by a 12.5pc jump for semiconductor tester Advantest.

articles.title: Islamabad United snap up Matt Henry, Karachi Kings secure Adil Rashid as direct signings for PSL 12
articles.summary:
Islamabad United have signed New Zealand fast bowler Matt Henry, while Karachi Kings have secured the services of England leg-spinner Adil Rashid as their marquee direct signings for the 12th edition of the Pakistan Super League (PSL).

Multan Sultans have also utilised the direct-signing facility, bringing Australian fast bowler Lance Morris on board ahead of the player auction scheduled for January 23, 2027.

Lahore Qalandars announced Sri Lankan batter Kamindu Mendis as their direct signing, while Quetta Gladiators have signed Lockie Ferguson.

Islamabad United unveiled Henry in an announcement on Tuesday, adding an experienced international campaigner to their bowling attack.

The 34-year-old New Zealand seamer has taken 199 Twenty20 wickets and is set to make his first appearance in the PSL after having featured in the Indian Premier League (IPL).

Karachi Kings, meanwhile, have opted for the experience of Rashid, a key member of England’s white-ball teams that won the 2019 ICC World Cup and the 2022 T20 World Cup.

The 38-year-old leg-spinner is renowned for his variations and ability to take wickets in the middle overs.

Although previously selected by Multan Sultans in a supplementary category, Rashid did not feature in the tournament after withdrawing due to international commitments. He will make his PSL debut with Karachi, with the deal reportedly valued at around Rs6.2 crore.

Multan Sultans have strengthened their pace department with the signing of Morris, nicknamed ‘The Wild Thing’ for his express pace.

The Australian right-arm fast bowler has limited international experience but has represented Melbourne Stars and Perth Scorchers in the Big Bash League. His ability to generate considerable pace is expected to bolster the Sultans’ bowling attack.

The direct-signing window, which opened on October 23 and closed on November 23, allowed each of the eight franchises to recruit one overseas marquee player who did not feature in either PSL 10 or PSL 11.

Under the regulations, a franchise making a direct signing will see its salary cap increase from Rs45 crore to Rs50.5 crore.

Each team can retain a maximum of seven players, including its direct signing, with the retention deadline set for January 13, 2027. Franchises retaining the full quota will be required to release one player from the highest price category of the previous auction into the general pool.

PSL 12 is scheduled to run from March 18 to May 2, 2027, with 44 matches planned across five to six venues.

articles.title: Govt reduces diesel price by Rs4 per litre, petrol by Re1 per litre
articles.summary:
The government on Tuesday reduced the price of petrol by Re1 per litre and that of diesel by Rs4 per litre, according to a notification by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra).

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs318 per litre and diesel at Rs353 per litre on Nov 25 (Wednesday).

The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.

Under an arrangement announced on Nov 2, for 30 days, oil refineries will contribute to the petroleum levy by bearing a cumulative impact of Rs15 billion, according to the government. This allows a Rs14.71 reduction in the petrol price at the consumer end.

On Sept 17, the government rolled out the Prime Minister’s Fuel Relief Scheme across the country to ease the public’s burden amid rising fuel prices due to the Middle East situation.

The subsidy scheme applies to owners of motorcycles, rickshaws and vehicles of up to 800cc.

Rise in fuel prices

The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28.

The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March.

Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50pc for three months.

Since July 17, the government has been revising fuel prices on a near-daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.

The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give Ogra the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.

Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the conflict. The federal government had also announced targeted relief measures in April to provide subsidised fuel.

Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.

Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

articles.title: PTI moves IHC for live broadcast of Al-Qadir Trust case hearing
articles.summary:
ISLAMABAD: The Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) has filed a petition in the Islamabad High Court (IHC), seeking live broadcast of the appeal proceedings in the £190 million Al-Qadir Trust case involving party founder Imran Khan.

Imran and his wife, Bushra Bibi, were convicted and sentenced in January 2025 in the corruption case. An accountability court found them guilty of receiving billions of rupees and hundreds of kanals of land from a real estate firm in exchange for legalising Rs50bn that had been identified and returned to Pakistan by the UK during the previous PTI government.

The petition was filed on Tuesday through Barristers Salman Safdar, Salman Akram Raja and other lawyers.

It argues that the case is a matter of national importance and that live broadcasting of Imran’s appeal proceedings is essential to ensure transparency, uphold justice and maintain public confidence in the judicial system.

Live coverage would allow the public to witness the proceedings firsthand and dispel speculation and misinformation, the petition states. It adds that justice must not only be done but must also be seen to be done.

The petition invokes Article 19-A of the Constitution, which guarantees citizens the right to access information on matters of public importance.

It also cites the live broadcast of the Zulfikar Ali Bhutto reference and proceedings in the Pervez Musharraf case before the Supreme Court. It notes that the IHC has previously issued directions for the live broadcast of proceedings in significant cases.

The petition also raises concerns about Imran’s alleged solitary confinement in prison, the denial of adequate medical facilities and restrictions on meetings with his family members and legal representatives.

It expresses concern over what it describes as prison authorities’ negligence regarding his medical condition, including blood pressure and treatment.

It further points out that details of the verdict and sentence in the Al-Qadir Trust case were reported in the media even before the formal announcement of the judgment, raising questions about the transparency of the judicial process.

The petition argues that live broadcasting would allow an independent assessment of all legal aspects of the case and requested the IHC to order the live broadcast of the complete proceedings of the appeal.

IHC has fixed November 25 for hearing appeals filed by Imran and Bushra against their convictions.

According to the cause list issued by the registrar’s office, a division bench comprising Chief Justice Sardar Mohammad Sarfraz Dogar and Justice Muhammad Asif will take up the appeals.

The PTI founder and Bushra Bibi have challenged their convictions in the high-profile case and sought relief from the high court.

Last month, senior members of the PTI legal team approached the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC), seeking early fixation of a criminal appeal filed by Bushra Bibi in the case.

The FCC rejected her plea seeking suspension of her seven-year sentence, observing that there were no sufficient grounds to interfere with an April 30 IHC order declining to suspend her sentence while her appeal remained pending.

Bushra, along with Imran, had initially moved the IHC for the suspension of her sentence in July last year. But the high court dismissed their requests in May 2026, observing that their appeals against their convictions had already been fixed for hearing.

articles.title: Rohail Nazir's fifty books Asia Cup Rising Stars semi-finals spot for Pakistan Shaheens
articles.summary:
An unbeaten half-century by Rohail Nazir, followed by a devastating bowling display, helped Pakistan Shaheens defeat Nepal by 96 runs in their final Group ‘B’ match of the Asia Cup Rising Stars at the University of Doha for Science and Technology on Tuesday.

The defending champions remained unbeaten in the tournament, winning all three of their group matches to qualify for the semi-finals, where they will face Bangladesh A on Nov 27.

Batting first, Pakistan Shaheens were in trouble at 66-6 in 16.5 overs before wicket-keeper-batter Rohail steadied the innings with an unbeaten 64 off 83 balls, hitting four fours and three sixes.

After Hasan Nawaz fell for 28 off 59 balls, leaving the Shaheens at 88-7, Rohail added 70 runs for the eighth wicket with Ahmed Daniyal, who scored 16 off 35 balls, to help his side reach 168 before being bowled out in 42 overs.

For Nepal, Rashid Khan claimed five wickets for 39 runs, while Abhishesh Gautam took two.

Nepal’s chase got off to a disastrous start as Muhammad Imran and Mohammad Hasnain reduced them to 15-4 inside six overs. Hasnain struck twice in successive deliveries to dismiss Ishan Pandey and Lokesh Bam without scoring.

Left-arm spinner Sufyan Moqim then claimed three wickets as Nepal slumped to 59-9. Mayan Yadav offered some resistance with a top score of 41 off 50 balls but was trapped leg-before by Maaz Sadaqat as Nepal were dismissed for 72 in 17.3 overs.

Hasnain and Sufyan took three wickets each for 21 and 17 runs respectively, while Imran claimed two for 29.

Rohail was named player of the match for his match-winning innings.

articles.title: Fazl decries ‘state siege’, claims prevented from attending Lahore event
articles.summary:
LAHORE: Police began removing barriers around Maulana Fazlur Rehman’s place of stay in Lahore on Tuesday evening, with the Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief claiming he had been put under an hours-long “state siege” to restrict his movement.

In a post at 10:40am, JUI-F said Fazl reached Lahore on Monday night and was scheduled to address lawyers today at a seminar at the invitation of the Lahore High Court Bar Association (LHCBA). However, due to police deployment, he was restricted from leaving his accommodation, JUI-F said.

JUI-F spokesperson Hafiz Ghazanfar Aziz said police began removing the hurdles by 7pm and informed Fazl that he was free to leave. However, the senior politician decided to stay in the city for the night.

Aziz condemned the alleged government action, calling it an attack on civil liberties and constitutional rights.

A city police officer, who spoke on condition of anonymity, also confirmed that police began “removing the barriers” by evening.

Meanwhile, a plea challenging the alleged “siege” of Fazl’s place of stay was filed in the Lahore High Court (LHC). On the other hand, the district administration also placed a three-day ban on public gatherings and “unlawful assemblies”.

In an earlier video message, the JUI-F chief alleged that he was under a “state siege” and that roadblocks and checkpoints across Lahore were preventing him from attending a multi-party seminar organised by the LHCBA.

Fazl thanked the bar association, its president and members for inviting him to address the seminar, but regretted that “state-imposed restrictions” had prevented him from attending in person.

He said the entire city had been “choked” by roadblocks and checkpoints, adding that peaceful citizens were being stopped from entering an environment of “intellectual discussion”.

“God willing, these sieges will break, these obstacles will be removed. Oppression never achieves permanence, but patience has always enjoyed permanence throughout history,” he said.

Fazl said his party had always worked for peace and had put its workers’ lives at risk for the country. He added that JUI-F did not need “a certificate of patriotism” from the rulers or any state institution.

“Neither from the rulers nor from any state institution have we come to obtain a certificate of loyalty to the homeland. In fact, I believe that perhaps we should be the ones issuing this certificate to people now. Their loyalties are questionable, whereas our loyalties are above all suspicion,” he said.

Claiming arrests of party workers and leaders in different areas, the JUI-F chief said his party would go ahead with its planned public conference in Sargodha on Nov 26.

He alleged that businesses were being shut down, shops and flour mills sealed, and party office-bearers arrested in Bhakkar, Mianwali, Khushab, Sargodha and its tehsils.

The JUI-F chief urged the public to make the gathering successful and demonstrate their commitment to freedom, constitutional supremacy, the rule of law and democracy.

“We are fighting the case of the public. We are fighting the case of Pakistan. We are fighting the case of this state,” he said.

Fazl alleged that the state had intensified its actions against JUI-F after the party exposed its role in matters concerning mineral resources in tribal areas.

He said his party was fighting for the rights of people across all provinces, including Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Balochistan, Sindh and Punjab, as well as Gwadar.

“These are the property of the people, not the property of the federation, nor the property of any single powerful institution, and we will not allow it to be looted by anyone,” he said.

Fazl said his party would remain steadfast in its position and take the matter to its “logical conclusion”. He reiterated his gratitude to the LHCBA and regretted that restrictions had prevented him from addressing its members directly.

Opposition leaders Mehmood Khan Achakzai and Allama Raja Nasir Abbas, PTI MNA Asad Qaiser, and veteran lawyer Ali Ahmed Kurd were among the participants of the LHCBA gathering, videos showed.

Plea filed in LHC against alleged ‘siege’

The plea against the alleged “siege” of Fazl’s accommodation was filed before the LHC by JUI-F lawyer Advocate Abrar Hussain.

It has yet to be fixed.

In his petition, the lawyer alleged that around 3,000 police personnel had been deployed outside Fazl’s residence, effectively confining him to his house.

The petitioner said he had sought a copy of the legal order authorising the detention or confinement of Fazl by police officials, but authorities did not share any such document.

He further alleged that police had also denied him permission to meet the JUI-F chief.

The petitioner requested the court to direct the police to lift the “siege” of Fazl’s residence.

In a statement, the party’s spokesperson warned that arrests of JUI-F workers in different cities on Monday, followed by the alleged deployment of a heavy police contingent outside the party chief’s residence, would have political consequences for the government.

He said arrests, roadblocks, the sealing of businesses and the registration of FIRs could not deter the party from its struggle. The JUI-F, he added, would continue its efforts for the supremacy of the Constitution and the protection of people’s rights.

Section 144 imposed in Lahore

Separately, Section 144 was imposed in Lahore for three days, from Nov 24 to 26, according to an order issued by the deputy commissioner, a copy of which is available with Dawn.

The order cited reports from law enforcement and intelligence agencies about a “serious and imminent threat” to public peace, security and the safety of life and property across Punjab, including Lahore, from militant and terrorist organisations and hostile intelligence agencies.

It said assemblies, rallies, gatherings, sit-ins, processions, demonstrations and public meetings could become targets for terrorist attacks, adding that the possibility of an untoward incident could not be ruled out.

The order also expressed apprehension that certain elements could engage in activities likely to lead to unlawful gatherings, disturb public order and pose security risks, potentially resulting in the loss of life and property or damage to critical infrastructure.

Under the restrictions, a complete ban has been imposed on the assembly of five or more people, processions and gatherings in any public place, street, road, highway, motorway or open space. The order also prohibits inciting people to participate in unlawful assemblies.

However, the restrictions will not apply to marriage ceremonies, funeral prayers, burial gatherings, prayers in mosques and churches, official duties of government and semi-government organisations, and courts of law, the order stated.

Fazl-govt rift
