articles.title: Katsina suspends Daura emir from official functions, probes sexual assault allegations
articles.summary:
From Agaju Madugba, Katsina

Katsina State Government has suspended all official engagements and travels of the Emir of Daura, Umar Farouk Umar, following allegations of sexual assault levelled against the traditional ruler by a Polish tourist who visited his palace on November 14, 2026.

Governor Dikko Umar Radda has also directed the establishment of a committee to investigate the allegations, which have generated widespread public outrage and attracted calls from human rights organisations and prominent Nigerians for an independent investigation to establish the circumstances surrounding the alleged incident and ensure that justice is served.

Commissioner for Information and Culture, Bala Salisu Zango, who announced the government’s decision in a statement yesterday, said the administration was taking the allegations seriously and would ensure the full implementation of the recommendations of the investigative committee.

“The state government has taken the allegations seriously. His Excellency Malam Dikko Umar Radda, has therefore directed for the establishment of a committee to investigate the issue and advise the government accordingly.

“Meanwhile, the state government has also suspended all official engagements and travels of the monarch.

“The government wishes to assure the public that justice will be served and that the outcome of the committee’s findings and recommendations will be fully implemented.

“Therefore, government wishes to call on the general public to be calm, law-abiding and continue with their normal activities.”

The government’s directive, however, did not announce the removal of the monarch from the throne, but restricted his official engagements and travels pending investigation.

•Genesis of the controversy

The controversy erupted at the weekend after the foreign tourist, a travel blogger who identifies herself as Mirka, took to social media to recount her alleged ordeal during a visit to the Daura palace as part of a 30-day tour of Nigeria.

The tourist, who had documented her visits to several communities and traditional institutions across the country, alleged that the monarch touched her breasts without her consent during an audience with him at his palace on Saturday, November 14.

She claimed that what began as a cordial reception subsequently degenerated into an uncomfortable encounter during which the traditional ruler allegedly hugged, kissed and touched her inappropriately despite her objections.

The tourist subsequently released video footage which she said was recorded with smart glasses during the encounter, explaining that she had deliberately waited until she left Nigeria before making her allegations public.

Before her visit to Daura, she had visited the palace of the Oba of Benin on October 24 and attended activities marking the 10th coronation anniversary of Oba Ewuare II the following day.

The footage generated widespread reactions on social media, with human rights advocates and other Nigerians demanding an investigation.

Following the controversy, the Daura Emirate Council announced on Monday that it had commenced a review of the video to establish its authenticity and determine whether it had been manipulated.

The council’s spokesperson, Ibrahim Murtala, confirmed in an interview with Channels Television that the emirate was aware of the footage and was examining the allegations.

The council indicated that it would issue a formal statement upon conclusion of its review.

However, an unnamed palace source had earlier dismissed the allegations, acknowledging that the tourist visited the palace but denying that any inappropriate conduct took place.

The Katsina State Police Command was also reported on Monday to have said it had not received a formal complaint concerning the alleged incident.

Amnesty International Nigeria had on Sunday called on the Katsina State Government and the Nigeria Police Force to immediately investigate the allegations, insisting that the status of the traditional ruler should not prevent the authorities from establishing the facts and ensuring accountability through due process.

The organisation stressed that the allegations presented an opportunity for the authorities to demonstrate their commitment to protecting women against sexual violence, irrespective of the social standing of those accused.

In a further intervention yesterday, Amnesty International raised the alarm over hundreds of death threats allegedly directed at the tourist following her decision to make the allegations public.

The organisation said the woman had been subjected to sustained cyberbullying, intimidation and abusive messages, including threats to kill or harm her unless she withdrew her allegations.

It condemned the harassment and called for the protection of her rights and safety, amid concerns that intimidation of complainants could discourage other victims of sexual violence from reporting their experiences.

Before yesterday’s announcement by the Katsina State Government, former military governor of Kaduna State, Col. Abubakar Dangiwa Umar (retd.), had called on Radda to suspend the monarch pending the outcome of a comprehensive, impartial and transparent investigation into the allegations.

In an open letter to the governor dated November 23, Umar argued that the traditional institution occupied an important position in society and that its custodians were expected to demonstrate exemplary conduct.

He maintained that suspending the monarch pending investigation would not amount to a declaration of guilt but would safeguard the integrity of the traditional institution and protect the investigative process.

The former military governor also recommended the deposition of the monarch should the authenticity of the footage and the allegations against him be established.

Similarly, the Human Rights Writers Association of Nigeria (HURIWA) called on the Inspector-General of Police and the Katsina State Government to ensure an impartial investigation, warning against allowing the monarch’s age, status or influence to obstruct the pursuit of justice.

Islamic cleric, Sheikh Ahmad Gumi, also joined those demanding accountability, advocating the removal of any traditional ruler found guilty of immoral conduct.

Umar ascended the throne on February 28, 2007, following the death of his predecessor, Muhammadu Bashar Dan Umaru, who had occupied the throne for 41 years.

He is recognised as the 60th traditional ruler of Daura and has been on the throne for more than 19 years.

Daura occupies a significant position in the history of northern Nigeria as one of the seven original Hausa states, traditionally known as the Hausa Bakwai, and is also the hometown of former President Muhammadu Buhari.

The emirate’s historical and cultural significance has made its palace a destination for diplomats, political leaders, researchers and tourists seeking to explore the heritage of northern Nigeria.

The allegations against the monarch have yet to be established by an independent investigation, while the composition, terms of reference and reporting deadline of the committee constituted by the Katsina State Government were not disclosed in the statement announcing the suspension of his official engagements.

The post Katsina suspends Daura emir from official functions, probes sexual assault allegations appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

articles.title: Plateau: Gunmen kill 11, 9 buried in mass grave
articles.summary:
From Jude Dangwam and Jude Owuamanam, Jos

At least 11 people were killed in separate attacks in Mangu and Bokkos local governments, Plateau State, with nine victims buried in a mass grave, while the burning of houses in neighbouring Qua’an Pan LG forced the council chairman to impose a curfew.

Among those killed was an Operation Rainbow commander who had recently completed a training programme in Jos. In a separate tragedy, a newly married couple died from burns sustained when fire engulfed their residence in Bukuru, Jos South Local Government Area.

The nine victims buried in a mass grave were killed during an attack on Zwagal village in Jipal District of Mangu LGA on Sunday night. Several houses were also razed at Bong community in Doemak District of Qua’an Pan LGA.

Local sources said the attackers, who reportedly arrived in their hundreds, stormed the hilltop communities, shooting residents, setting houses ablaze, looting property and stealing livestock.

Some of the animals were reportedly butchered by the attackers, who were said to have operated for several hours.

The village head of Zwagal, Jonathan Wadong, said the attack began at about 8 p.m. on Sunday, when sporadic gunshots shattered the peace of the community.

Wadong alleged that the attackers were Fulani militias, saying: “They were speaking Fulani language.”

He appealed to the government to deploy adequate security personnel to protect residents and prevent further attacks. He also commended the chairmen of Mangu and Qua’an Pan local LGAs  for promptly mobilising security personnel to the affected communities.

The burning of houses at Bong reportedly triggered panic in other parts of Qua’an Pan, with residents fleeing Doemak, the local government headquarters, amid fears of further attacks.

The Chairman of Qua’an Pan Local Government Council, Christopher Audu Manship, imposed a curfew late Monday evening to contain the situation and prevent a further breakdown of law and order.

Manship, who visited the affected communities, witnessed the mass burial at Zwagal alongside the Chairman of Mangu Local Government Council, Emmanuel Bala Mwolpun.

Describing the attacks as barbaric and inhuman, he reaffirmed the government’s commitment to tackling insecurity and urged residents, particularly youths, to remain vigilant and promptly report suspicious movements to security agencies.

During an assessment of the destruction at Bong, Manship assured residents that the government would not abandon them, pledging support for rebuilding their homes and strengthening security.

He also disclosed that efforts were being made to improve telecommunications coverage in the community to facilitate timely communication, security surveillance and monitoring.

In Bokkos LGA, gunmen killed two men in an ambush at about 3 p.m. on Monday as they returned from a condolence visit to Hurti village.

The victims were travelling to their community in Tadai, Manguna District, when they were attacked.

A community leader, Machief Paul, who confirmed the incident, said both victims were members of his community. He disclosed that one of them had recently completed a training programme for Operation Rainbow unit commanders.

“One of the victims was a newly graduated commander of Operation Rainbow who had recently completed a refresher training programme for unit commanders in Jos. He was agile and ready for the job, but unfortunately his career has been cut short,” Paul said.

Meanwhile, a newly married couple, Sikiru Habib and his wife, Ramlat Lawan, have died after suffering severe burns when fire engulfed their residence in Anguwan Miyango, Bukuru, Jos South LGA.

The fire reportedly broke out at about 2:30 a.m. on Saturday while the couple were asleep. Residents suspected a power surge, although the actual cause of the fire had yet to be established.

A neighbour, Lawal Suleiman, said residents woke up to discover the raging inferno and found that the door to the couple’s room would not open, trapping them inside as young men in the neighbourhood struggled to rescue them.

He said the rescuers eventually broke the window and brought the couple out before firefighters arrived to provide emergency assistance.

The victims were rushed to the Jos University Teaching Hospital, where Habib died on Sunday, while his wife succumbed to her injuries on Monday.

The post Plateau: Gunmen kill 11, 9 buried in mass grave appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

articles.title: Benue police arrest 26 suspects, kill 3 bandits
articles.summary:
From Scholastica Hir, Makurdi

The Benue State Police Command has arrested 26 suspects, neutralised three suspected bandits and rescued five kidnapped persons in separate security operations across the state.

Among those arrested are nine suspects allegedly involved in the killing of a 52-year-old man, Felix Ahemba, whose body was dumped in a cassava farm at Tyo Adu Village, Gboko Local Government Area (LGA) of the state.

The police also recovered four locally made firearms, 495 rounds of live ammunition, 290 ammunition chains, a stolen Toyota Camry, a Honda motorcycle, assorted charms and a locally made knife during the operations.

The Commissioner of Police, Cletus Nwadiogbu, disclosed this while briefing journalists  yesterday at the Command headquarters in Makurdi.

He said the successes were recorded through intelligence-led operations, proactive policing and collaboration with other security agencies.

Nwadiogbu disclosed that operatives of the Katsina-Ala Division, working in collaboration with the Police Mobile Force and Operation Whirl Stroke (OPWS), rescued five persons abducted at Utange Village, Tor-Donga District, Katsina-Ala LGA, on November 8.

He, however, regretted that three of the rescued victims, who sustained severe injuries during the incident, died while being conveyed to hospital, while the remaining two survived.

The police commissioner also disclosed that 10 suspects were arrested in connection with the abduction of a commercial driver, Mohammed Musa, a woman and her six-year-old son at Ojinebe-Adoka Village.

He said operatives of the Violent Crime Response Unit arrested the suspects on November 7, adding that the vehicle in which the victims were last seen was later discovered burnt along the route.

According to him, efforts are ongoing to locate the three missing persons and apprehend other suspects still at large.

On the fight against armed robbery, Nwadiogbu said two suspects, Saviour Shagbaor and Maakaven Matthew, were arrested in Gboko following an attack on a commercial motorcyclist and his passenger.

He said the assailants allegedly used a locally made firearm during the attack before escaping with the victim’s Bajaj motorcycle.

He further disclosed that two other suspects, Michael Tyonongu and Godwin Agaibge, were arrested along the Gbajimgba-Makurdi Road on November 16, with a locally fabricated pistol.

Another suspect, Tersoo Orjime, was arrested in Makurdi over an alleged attempted robbery, with a locally made revolver pistol and a knife recovered from him.

The CP added that a suspected cult member, Dan Azumi Audu, was arrested at Yagba Community, Makurdi, following a distress call. A locally fabricated revolver pistol and live ammunition were recovered from him.

Nwadiogbu also announced the arrest of a suspected car-snatching suspect, Anthony Nagu, by operatives of Operation Zenda at Otukpa, where a red Toyota Camry allegedly stolen from Badagry, Lagos State, was recovered.

On the burning of the Traditional Council Hall at Tyem-Imongu Community in Vandeikya LGA on November 4, the police commissioner said nine persons had been arrested in connection with the incident.

He disclosed that investigation had been concluded and the suspects charged to court.

On the arrest of suspected bandits and recovery of ammunition, Nwadiogbu said operatives of Operation Zenda intercepted a vehicle travelling from Jato-Aka towards Makurdi through Gboko on November 15.

He said a passenger identified as Shawon Order Timothy was arrested during the operation, while 490 rounds of ammunition of different calibres and 290 ammunition chains were recovered from him.

The suspect, according to the CP, was allegedly linked to the killing of security personnel at Agu Centre on September 19, 2025.

He said the suspect remained in custody as investigations continued.

Nwadiogbu urged residents to remain vigilant and provide credible and timely information to security agencies, stressing that lasting security could only be achieved through the cooperation of all stakeholders.

He reaffirmed the Command’s commitment to sustaining intelligence gathering, strengthening security operations and ensuring the safety of the people.

The post Benue police arrest 26 suspects, kill 3 bandits appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

articles.title: Offa robbery: Saraki, Ahmed’s arraignment stalled till December 3
articles.summary:
From Taiwo Ogunniyi, Ilorin

The planned arraignment of former Senate President Bukola Saraki and former Kwara State Governor Abdulfatah Ahmed over the Offa robbery case suffered a setback yesterday as a Kwara State High Court, Ilorin ruled that proceedings could not commence until the defendants had been properly served with the charges against them.

The court, presided over by Justice Osuolale Ajayi, rejected the prosecution’s bid to proceed immediately with the arraignment, upholding the defence’s objection that serving the charges on the defendants’ lawyers did not satisfy the legal requirement for personal service and fair hearing.

Justice Ajayi consequently directed the prosecution to ensure that the charges were served on the defendants on or before November 20 and adjourned the matter until December 3, 2026, for arraignment.

The ruling followed arguments by the prosecution and defence teams at the previous sitting, during which the court reserved its decision on the procedural objections raised against the commencement of proceedings.

The prosecution had urged the court to arraign the four defendants without further delay, arguing that the trial should commence immediately.

However, the defence opposed the application, insisting that the defendants had not been personally served with the charges and that proceeding with their arraignment under the circumstances would violate due process and their constitutional right to a fair hearing.

At the previous sitting, counsel to Saraki, Adebayo Adelodun, SAN, had questioned the urgency surrounding the proceedings and challenged the manner in which the prosecution sought to bring the defendants before the court.

“My Lord, why the hurry?” Adelodun asked.

He also drew the court’s attention to a pending appeal challenging issues relating to jurisdiction and the competence of the trial court to entertain the case.

The defence urged the court to take cognisance of the appellate proceedings and the legal objections before taking further steps in the matter.

Justice Ajayi, however, declined to suspend proceedings on account of the pending appeal, explaining that there was no indication of when the Court of Appeal would deliver its ruling on the defence’s application seeking an order directing the parties to maintain the status quo ante bellum.

Meanwhile, the Court of Appeal, Ilorin has reserved its ruling on an application filed by Saraki and Ahmed seeking to compel the parties and the trial court to maintain the status quo ante bellum pending the determination of their appeal.

The application before the appellate court is separate from the issue of service of charges decided by the High Court.

With the latest ruling, the prosecution must comply with the November 20 deadline for service of the charges before the trial court can proceed with the planned arraignment on December 3.

The post Offa robbery: Saraki, Ahmed’s arraignment stalled till December 3 appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

articles.title: Idris’ family fights over late Kogi ex-gov’s multi-billion estate
articles.summary:
From Godwin Tsa, Abuja

A battle over the estate of the late former Governor of Kogi State, Alhaji Ibrahim Idris, has opened at an Upper Area Court in Abuja. Four of his children are asking the court to freeze his properties and appoint a receiver/manager to take charge of them.

In suit CV/101/2026, Asma’u, Fatima, Zainab and Jamila Ibrahim Idris are asking the court to restrain 13 other family members from selling, leasing, mortgaging, gifting, transferring or otherwise dealing with any part of the estate.

The respondents include Hajiya Aisha, Abubakar, Abdullahi, Sulaiman, Hussaini, Abdurahman, Idris (Atayi), Ibrahim, Hassan, Iman, Iram and Ilan Ibrahim Idris.

In a motion marked M/46/2026, filed by their lawyer, I. H. Nalaraba, and brought under sections 6(6)(b) and 272(1) of the 1999 Constitution and the court’s inherent jurisdiction, the applicants want an interlocutory injunction pending the determination of the substantive suit.

Properties in dispute

The properties listed include:

Grand Ibro Hotel and its Annex, both in Wuse Zone 5, Abuja; A house on Kwame Nkrumah Street, Asokoro, Abuja;

A house behind Government House, Lokoja; A house in Idah; Landed properties in Lokoja, Idah, Ayingba and Abejukolo.

Others are; a one-bedroom apartment in Dubai; Land behind SETRACO, Jabi, Abuja; Bank accounts in several Nigerian banks; The late governor’s personal effects, including cars, clothes, wristwatches, footwear and furniture.

The applicants want a receiver/manager to take over, preserve and manage the estate and collect its rents and income. They want the receiver to file a full inventory of the properties, within and outside Abuja, within 21 days of appointment. He would open a dedicated estate account in a reputable bank and file accounts of his stewardship every three months. He would also be barred from disposing of any property without the court’s leave, and paid a remuneration fixed by the court out of the estate’s income.

They also want the respondents, and any other heir who has collected rent or income or taken possession of any item since the governor’s death on September 20, 2026, to account for it and return it to the receiver within 14 days.

The applicants further want tenants, managers, staff and bankers of the estate properties, including the management of Grand Ibro Hotel, to deal only with the receiver.

They want the respondents ordered to preserve all title documents, bank statements, receipts and tenancy agreements, and an accelerated hearing of the main suit.

In a 16-paragraph affidavit, Sani Sambo, a lawyer in the applicants’ counsel’s firm, said the estate has not been shared among the heirs according to Islamic law, although the deceased was a practising Muslim.

He said some respondents and other family members have been collecting rents from the hotel and other properties. They have also allegedly taken the late governor’s cars, wristwatches and other belongings, to the exclusion of the other heirs.

Sambo also alleged that a mosque at the hotel was demolished after the governor’s death and new construction begun by some family members. He added that the hotel business continues to run without any accounting to the family.

The applicants have also applied for a plaint seeking a declaration of the deceased’s heirs and an order sharing the estate under Islamic law.

Judge Ado Muktar has directed all the family members to appear in court on November 23, the next adjourned date, when an inventory of the estate is also to be taken.

The post Idris’ family fights over late Kogi ex-gov’s multi-billion estate appeared first on The Sun Nigeria.

articles.title: Female soldiers critical to Army operations –COAS
articles.summary:
From Noah Ebije, Kaduna

The Chief of Army Staff (COAS), Lt.-Gen. Waidi Shaibu, has said that developing the professional capabilities of female personnel is essential to strengthening the Nigerian Army’s capacity to accomplish its operational missions.

Shaibu stated this at the Nigerian Army Women Command’s Fourth Quarter 2026 Workshop held on Tuesday in Kaduna.

He was represented at the event by Maj.-Gen. Oladele Arogundade, Commander, Command Engineering Depot.

The workshop was themed: “Harnessing the Professional Capabilities of Nigerian Army Female Personnel in Support of Nigerian Army Operational Engagements in a Joint and Multi-Agency Environment.”

The COAS said the contemporary security environment continued to present complex and evolving challenges that required a highly professional, adaptive and resilient military force.

He noted that the professional capabilities of female officers and soldiers constituted an important component of the Nigerian Army’s human resources, stressing that their effective development and deployment were essential to strengthening the institution’s capacity to accomplish assigned missions.

According to him, operations against insurgency and terrorism, protection of vulnerable communities, internal security tasks and responses to humanitarian emergencies cannot be achieved through kinetic operations alone.

He said such operations required sound intelligence, cultural awareness, effective communication, discipline, civilian engagement and the ability to build confidence among affected populations.

Shaibu explained that during engagements with communities where cultural or religious sensitivities influenced who could freely interact with residents, the presence of trained female personnel could provide access that might otherwise be difficult to achieve.

He cited the contributions of female personnel during stabilisation operations in Jos North in April, where they served as force multipliers in efforts to restore peace and security following a breakdown of law and order in the Angwan Ruba area.

He said their professional conduct attracted commendation, noting that they demonstrated resilience and competence while performing operational duties alongside their male counterparts.

“The Nigerian Army remains committed to advancing professionalism, meritocracy and operational competencies across all its formations and units,” he said.

The COAS stressed that the development of female personnel must be anchored on established military standards, appropriate training and opportunities for professional growth.

He said the workshop would address critical areas, including identifying and developing professional capabilities, expanding opportunities in combat, specialist and leadership appointments, as well as adaptive leadership, mentorship and career progression.

Other areas, he said, included critical thinking, decision-making, peace support operations, humanitarian assistance and civil-military relations.

He urged participants to move beyond theoretical discussions and produce practical recommendations that would strengthen the professional development and effective deployment of female personnel.

“I wish to emphasise that expanding professional opportunities must be firmly anchored on competence, merit and established military standards,” he said.

Shaibu explained that the objective was not merely to increase the number of female personnel in particular appointments but to ensure that suitably qualified officers and soldiers were adequately prepared and effectively deployed.

He added that discipline, integrity and resourcefulness remained fundamental to military functionality and operational effectiveness.

Earlier, the Acting Commander, Nigerian Army Women Command, Col. Sule Ahmed, said the workshop’s theme reflected the importance of developing and effectively utilising the professional capabilities of female personnel to meet contemporary operational requirements.

Ahmed said the workshop was in line with the United Nations Women, Peace and Security Agenda, particularly United Nations Security Council Resolution 1325 of 2000, which underscores women’s participation in conflict prevention, conflict resolution, peacebuilding and security processes.

He disclosed that the workshop would also address drug and substance abuse, as well as mental health management, particularly their implications for personnel welfare and operational efficiency.

Ahmed thanked the Chief of Army Staff for approving and supporting the workshop.

In his lecture, retired Maj.-Gen. Adeniyi Oyebade said operational success depended on men and women working effectively together, rather than on women alone.

He stressed that the issue was not simply about women’s participation but about harnessing the complementary strengths of both sexes to improve operational outcomes.

“The women cannot do it alone, that is the truth, but when you have the men there, it enhances the operational capacity and they can deliver effectively on the outcomes,” he said.

Oyebade also stressed the need to expose female personnel to the same training opportunities as their male counterparts, particularly in emerging areas of warfare.

Citing the changing nature of modern battlefields, especially the ongoing war in Ukraine, he said drone technology had become central to military operations, with women playing significant roles as drone operators.

“Look at what is happening in Ukraine, the use of drone technologies. Many of the drone operators are women,” he said.

He observed that women had demonstrated proficiency in drone operations because the technology required precision, attention to detail and fine-tuning of operations.

According to him, modern warfare is no longer determined solely by physical strength.

“Once you start moving away from physical effectiveness and strength and start seeing what women can bring, you will achieve more,” he said.

Oyebade commended the Commander, Nigerian Army Women Command, and the Chief of Army Staff for organising the Fourth Quarter workshop.

He urged the Command to involve male officers in subsequent training programmes to enable both sexes to share perspectives, learn from one another and draw strength from their complementary capabilities.

articles.title: Omo-Agege kicks against disqualification, heads to A‘Court
articles.summary:
• Says judgment defies facts, law, logic

• Court orders INEC to delist ex-DSP, forecloses fresh primary

 

From Joe Obukata Ogbodu, Warri

Former deputy Senate president, Ovie Omo-Agege, has rejected the judgment of the Federal High Court sitting in Warri, Delta State, nullifying his nomination as the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) candidate for Delta Central Senatorial District in the 2027 general elections, describing the verdict as one that defies facts, law and logic and directing his legal team to immediately challenge it at the Court of Appeal.

Omo-Agege, who suffered the judicial setback a day after an attack on his campaign entourage left six persons dead, according to preliminary police reports, and several others injured, insisted that the findings of the court were inconsistent with the documentary evidence presented before it, particularly the NDC membership register which, he said, contained his name and was authenticated by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).

Justice Hyeladzira Ajiya Nganjiwa had, in his judgment yesterday, ordered INEC to remove Omo-Agege’s name from its list of candidates and restrained him from parading himself as the NDC senatorial candidate, holding that his name was not contained in the party’s membership register submitted to the commission at least 21 days before its primary election.

In a further setback for the NDC, the court held that the party could no longer conduct a fresh primary to nominate another candidate for the senatorial seat, as the statutory window prescribed by the Electoral Act had elapsed.

However, Omo-Agege faulted the basis of the judgment, insisting that both the NDC and INEC presented documentary evidence establishing his membership of the party, while questioning the legal standing of the plaintiff, Prof. Alexander Osondu Akpodiete, to challenge the outcome of a primary election in which he allegedly neither sought the party’s nomination nor participated.

The former deputy senate president cautioned those celebrating the verdict as the end of his political journey against premature jubilation, declaring that the legal process had not run its course and that he would pursue every lawful avenue to overturn the judgment.

In a statement by his media aide, Sunny Areh, titled: “Warri judgment defies facts, law and logic; immediate appeal underway,” Omo-Agege expressed deep disappointment over the verdict but reaffirmed his commitment to the rule of law.

“While we respect the court, we strongly disagree with its decision. We believe that some of the findings do not reflect the documentary evidence presented before the court. Senator Omo-Agege has therefore directed his legal team to immediately challenge the judgment at the Court of Appeal.

“We are confident in the strength of our position and will pursue every lawful avenue to ensure that the issues raised by this judgment receive proper judicial consideration.”

Faulting the principal ground upon which the court invalidated his nomination, Omo-Agege maintained that the finding that his name was not contained in the NDC membership register was difficult to reconcile with the evidence presented before the court.

“Both the NDC and INEC produced documents showing that Senator Omo-Agege’s name was in the membership register submitted by the party. There was only one register. The NDC did not submit two different registers or maintain competing membership records for the same primary election. Senator Omo-Agege’s name appeared in the register submitted to INEC.

“Indeed, INEC acknowledged receipt of the register and issued Certified True Copies (CTCs) of that same document, bearing Senator Omo-Agege’s name, to several persons.

“The question that the Court of Appeal will be asked to examine is straightforward: if the register was before the trial court, and both the party and INEC presented evidence confirming that Senator Omo-Agege’s name appeared in it, what was the basis for the court’s contrary finding? This is a fundamental issue that deserves careful judicial scrutiny.”

Omo-Agege also questioned Akpodiete’s locus standi to institute the action, alleging that the plaintiff neither obtained the nomination forms required to participate in the party’s primary nor secured clearance from the NDC to contest the election.

According to him, Akpodiete’s name did not appear among the participants listed in INEC’s official monitoring report on the primary election.

“These circumstances raise serious questions about whether he established the legal standing required to challenge the outcome of a primary in which he did not participate. The issue is not whether a person can approach the courts for redress, but whether the plaintiff in this particular case demonstrated a sufficient legal interest to bring the action. We believe this issue warrants proper consideration on appeal.”

The statement further questioned the plaintiff’s decision to seek the invalidation of Omo-Agege’s nomination without asking the court to declare him the winner of the primary or award him the party’s ticket.

“It is also significant that the plaintiff did not ask the court to declare him the winner of the primary or award him the NDC ticket. Instead, he sought to invalidate the party’s nomination without seeking the ticket for himself. The implications of that position, including the legal interest behind the action, deserve close examination.”

Omo-Agege also alleged that attempts had been made before the judgment to persuade INEC to remove his name from its final list of candidates but that the commission declined, having confirmed that his name appeared in the membership register submitted by the NDC.

“These are official records, not political assertions. They formed part of the documentary evidence surrounding the case and must be examined in their proper context.”

•Why court nullified nomination

The judgment followed a suit instituted by Akpodiete, marked FHC/WR/CS/120/2026, challenging the validity of Omo-Agege’s nomination on grounds bordering on his resignation from the All Progressives Congress (APC), membership of the NDC and eligibility to participate in the party’s senatorial primary.

Delivering judgment, Justice Nganjiwa dismissed all five preliminary objections raised by Omo-Agege, the NDC and INEC challenging the competence of the suit before proceeding to determine the substantive issues raised by the plaintiff.

The court held that the NDC failed to comply with the mandatory provisions of the Electoral Act regarding the submission of its membership register to INEC ahead of its primary election, finding that Omo-Agege’s name was not contained in the register submitted to the commission within the prescribed period.

The judge further held that the party failed to provide credible evidence establishing that its membership register was subsequently updated to accommodate Omo-Agege and submitted to INEC within the statutory period preceding the primary.

Relying on INEC’s revised electoral timetable, the court also noted that Omo-Agege participated in the APC senatorial primary held on May 18, 2026, a development which, according to the court, established that he was still a member of the APC at the material time.

Justice Nganjiwa maintained that only persons whose names appeared in a political party’s membership register, in accordance with the requirements of the Electoral Act, were eligible to participate in its primary elections.

On the admissibility of a previously withdrawn affidavit, the court held that a party was entitled to withdraw an affidavit already filed in a proceeding, adding that once withdrawn, such an affidavit ceased to form part of the court’s records and could not be relied upon in determining the matter.

The judge maintained that a valid nomination could not be founded on a process that failed to satisfy statutory requirements, stressing that where a political party failed to comply with the Electoral Act in nominating its candidate, INEC was not permitted to include such a candidate on the ballot.

The court further held that the statutory window for conducting fresh primaries had closed, citing the provision of the Electoral Act prescribing a timeline of 180 days before the general elections.

Consequently, the court invalidated Omo-Agege’s nomination, directed INEC to delist him and restrained him from presenting himself as the NDC candidate for Delta Central Senatorial District in the forthcoming elections.

•My political journey not over – Omo-Agege

While reaffirming his respect for the judiciary, Omo-Agege maintained that exercising his right of appeal should not be construed as an attack on the court or rejection of the rule of law.

“Senator Omo-Agege has always maintained respect for the judiciary. That respect, however, does not require him to agree with every decision, particularly one he believes is inconsistent with the evidence and the applicable law. The right of appeal is an essential part of our judicial system. Exercising that right is neither an attack on the court nor a rejection of the rule of law.

“He has therefore directed his legal team to proceed immediately to the Court of Appeal. We intend to challenge the findings of the trial court and seek the correction of what we regard as serious errors in the judgment.”

The former deputy senate president insisted that the verdict would not diminish his commitment to the NDC and the people of Delta Central.

“Those already celebrating this decision as the end of Senator Omo-Agege’s political journey should exercise patience. This is a judgment of the trial court, and the opportunity for appellate review remains. The legal process has not run its course.

“Our commitment to the NDC and the people of Delta Central remains firm. Senator Omo-Agege will not abandon the democratic process because of a judgment he believes to be wrong. He will defend his rights through the courts and remain committed to the people whose support has brought him this far.

“We believe in the rule of law, but we also believe that justice must be anchored in facts and evidence. We will appeal this judgment and pursue that appeal with determination.”

•Double setback

The judgment came amid heightened tension over Monday’s deadly attack on Omo-Agege’s campaign entourage at Uduere community, which prompted the Delta State Government to impose an indefinite dusk-to-dawn curfew across Ughelli North Local Government Area.

The incident triggered a war of words between Omo-Agege’s campaign organisation and the state government, with the former accusing Governor Sheriff Oborevwori and the Chairman of Ughelli North Local Government Area, Jaro Egbo, of complicity in the attack.

The state government dismissed the allegations and vowed to ensure that those responsible for the killings were brought to justice, irrespective of their political positions or status.

The Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Disu, has since ordered a thorough, impartial and evidence-based investigation into the attack, including the conduct of police personnel deployed to the venue.

As of press time, separate responses from the NDC and INEC to the judgment were not immediately available, while confirmation that Omo-Agege’s legal team had formally filed the appeal was still being awaited.

articles.title: Nigeria’s oil revenue safe as crude prices fall to 3-month low
articles.summary:
Nigeria’s oil revenue outlook remains relatively secure despite the fall in global crude prices to a three-month low.

Oil prices fell for a second consecutive day on Tuesday as rising global supplies and fears of a possible glut outweighed concerns over disruptions to crude shipments in the Middle East.

Brent crude futures dropped 75 cents, or 0.8 per cent, to $88.62 per barrel by 9:15 GMT, after hitting their lowest level since August 27.

Similarly, US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude fell 64 cents, or 0.8 per cent, to $79.53 per barrel, after sliding to its weakest level since August 10.

The price is above the Federal Government’s 2026 budget benchmark of $64.85 per barrel.

The price cushion offers some relief to the government amid concerns over falling oil prices, although the country’s ability to meet its production target remains critical to maximising earnings from crude exports and supporting the nation’s finances.

The decline in global prices came despite continued tensions around the Strait of Hormuz, a major global oil shipping route, where Iran’s Revolutionary Guards navy said three oil tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines on Monday.

The United States is also investigating possible Iranian involvement in cyberattacks targeting as many as 50 energy tankers, according to a report by the Wall Street Journal.

However, improving supply conditions have put pressure on prices, with Libya’s Sharara oil pipeline reopening after a disruption, allowing crude to flow into storage facilities.

China and India are also increasing their purchases of Russian oil, helping to make up for supply disruptions caused by the conflict involving Iran.

Analysts said the combination of rising supplies, strategic oil reserve releases and expectations of increased global production had weakened the support that geopolitical tensions previously provided for oil prices.

UBS analyst, Giovanni Staunovo, said oil prices were facing downward pressure as markets reduced their concerns about immediate geopolitical risks, while releases from strategic reserves were helping to keep supplies adequate despite lower exports from the Middle East.

He said the market was also weighing the possibility of excess supply against continuing tensions and shipping disruptions in the region.

Deutsche Bank said global oil and liquid fuel inventories rose by 52 million barrels in October, suggesting that supply exceeded demand by about 1.7 million barrels per day.

The bank said growing evidence showed that the global oil market was moving towards a surplus, although further disruptions could delay the trend.

Meanwhile, a preliminary Reuters poll indicated that US crude oil and petroleum product inventories were likely to have increased in the previous week, adding to concerns about oversupply.

However, analysts warned that the market remained vulnerable to fresh disruptions.

Daniel Hynes, senior commodity strategist at ANZ, said oil prices and other market indicators suggested that investors were increasingly expecting supply conditions to return to normal.

He, however, warned that shipping constraints and limited inventory buffers meant the market remained exposed to further shocks.

Suvro Sarkar, head of energy research at DBS Bank, also warned that oil prices could rise again depending on the outcome of talks between the United States and Iran and possible moves by both sides over the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Watch: Gaza declares meningitis alert as health ministry blames Israeli restrictions
articles.summary:
Watch: Gaza declares meningitis alert as health ministry blames Israeli restrictions

Gaza’s health ministry has issued an "epidemiological alert" across the territory, warning that a "shocking" increase in meningitis infections puts hundreds of thousands of lives at risk, particularly children.

 

The ministry urged the World Health Organization and Unicef to launch an emergency response.

 

Dr Nidal Ghunaim, deputy director general of primary healthcare for public health, reported 272 cases in October. He described the figure as more than eight times the usual monthly average of 30 to 50.

 

Meningitis has killed 15 people this year, Ghunaim said, including five during the surge from August to October.

 

The ministry described the outbreak as an "inevitable result of the destruction of infrastructure, overcrowding of shelters, mixing of drinking water with sewage, and the disaster being exacerbated by flooding due to rain".

articles.title: Who wins from Baghdad's move to clip Kurdish autonomy - the US or Iran?
articles.summary:
Who wins from Baghdad's move to clip Kurdish autonomy - the US or Iran?

Submitted by
Sean Mathews
on
Tue, 11/24/2026 - 21:41

Iraq's federal government said it was moving to seize control of border posts and energy facilities controlled by the KRG

Iranian trucks waiting to cross back into Iran in the Penjwen district in Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdistan Region in September 2026 (Safin Hamid/AFP)

Off

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has said Baghdad will take over all of Kurdistan's border crossings and several oil fields that the autonomous region controls, in a move that was widely condemned by the region’s leaders as a step to clip their autonomy.

Baghdad’s decision comes at a time of internal division in the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) and as the Middle East braces for a potential new US-Israeli attack on Iran.

Under American pressure, Zaidi recently attempted to crack down on Kataib Hezbollah, a powerful Shia militia in Iraq aligned with Iran, which officials in Baghdad say has earned hundreds of millions of dollars from smuggling oil.

Zaidi's spokesperson Sabah al-Numan said on Tuesday that, based on those findings, Baghad would take control of "all border crossings in the Kurdistan Region".

He added that Zaidi directed the oil ministry "to manage all oil fields" that are under Kurdish "security authority" despite lying outside the Kurdistan Region, in the provinces of Diyala, Kirkuk, Salaheddine and Nineveh. Zaidi also ordered the Kurdistan government not to approve oil exports except through the federal oil ministry.

The KRG is guaranteed some autonomy under Iraq’s 2005 constitution, but its control of border crossings has been a longstanding issue of dispute, as have energy resources. 

Does Iran or the US benefit?

The move by Baghdad’s central government to wrest control of the posts alongside energy facilities comes as it tries to seal new energy deals with Turkey and looks to pipelines through the region to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.

The KRG region has been a close US security partner for decades, but the last US troops left Erbil, the region's capital, in September, completing a full US withdrawal from Iraq. The region faced hundreds of Iranian missile and drone strikes during this year's war.

Inside the Iraqi Kurdish city caught between the US and Iran

Read More »

Experts debated whether Baghdad's decision was made with the agreement of Iran, which has called on the KRG to rein in Kurdish opposition groups, or the US which has lobbied regional states to consolidate federal power.

Tom Barrack, the US ambassador to Turkey and Middle East envoy, has been the main proponent of this view.

Yesar Al-Maleki, a Gulf analyst at the Middle East Economic Survey, said Zaidi was taking advantage of a shift in the US.

“Washington, has clearly shifted its Iraq policy toward greater centralisation; the PUK and KDP are no longer presenting a united front in Iraqi politics; and the US military withdrawal has given Baghdad greater security bandwidth,” he wrote on X.

'Tehran fears an uprising'

But Fabrice Balanche, a Kurdish expert, said Baghdad’s move would benefit Iran as well, given its suspicion of the US and Israel using the region as a base to attack it.

“Iraq’s determination to dismantle the KRG by depriving it of its economic resources must be seen in the context of the conflict between the US and Iran,” he wrote in an essay.

“Tehran fears that Iraqi Kurdistan could serve as a rear base for an uprising in Iranian Kurdistan,” he added.

The KRG is at its weakest in years. The region is dominated by two family dynasties, the Barzani family in Erbil, which leads the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), and the Talabani family in Sulaymaniyah, which leads the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK).

The PUK withdrew from the region's parliament in November and its leader, Bafel Talabani, said the region was already living "the reality of two governments and two administrations".

Kurdistan Region Prime Minister Masrour Barzani said his government was "surprised" by Zaidi's decisions, calling them "completely unacceptable".

But both parties put aside their differences to issue a relatively mild censure of Baghdad’s decision.

“The Kurdistan Region has never sought anything beyond the rights guaranteed to it under the Iraqi Constitution. However, its constitutional rights have been violated over the years,” the statement said.

“We stress that all parties must abide by the Constitution and that, should any dispute arise between the Kurdistan Region and the Federal Government, the Constitution must serve as the ultimate point of reference,” the statement added.

A report from the Office of The Inspector General has raised concerns that the US has given Israel an 'exemption' from the Leahy Law

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio pictured last month (Oliver Contreras/AFP)

Off

The US Department of State has a 12-year backlog of alleged cases of gross human rights violations in Israel to adjudicate, because the agency has made little effort to trace the end point of US military assistance there, a report quietly posted online by the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) last month showed. 

The findings "demonstrate that the Department has created an unlawful de facto exemption to the law for Israel", Charles Blaha, a state department official who retired in 2023, wrote in a piece for Just Security on Monday.

The OIG report hones in on the application of the Leahy Law, which prohibits US assistance to any foreign security forces unit if the secretary of state has credible information that such a unit has committed "gross violations of human rights". 

In a September 2025 report to Congress, the state department said the only units it had assessed to be ineligible for US security assistance were in Ukraine, Egypt and Jordan - even though Israel had previously been cited as having non-traceable assistance (NTA). 

The NTA means the state department "cannot identify recipient units in advance of the transfer of assistance or training, or the units are not known with sufficient detail to make Leahy vetting possible", the OIG report said. 

It concluded that the state department "had not developed or distributed comprehensive guidance and training to help staff implement NTA vetting requirements", and that nearly half of all missions overseas "did not respond to annual requirements to certify if a country was receiving NTA".

"For those countries receiving NTA, additional certifications are necessary to validate that foreign security forces are complying with US requirements," the report added. 

In April 2024, under the Biden administration, the state department determined that five Israeli security units had committed grave human rights violations.

But it then said that four of them had remedied the violations, and could still receive US security assistance, while the fifth unit would "remain indefinitely eligible while the State Department engaged with the government of Israel 'on identifying a path to effective remediation of this unit'". 

But the state department "has never delivered a list of ineligible Israeli units to the government of Israel. Not once", Blaha wrote in June of that year.

War on Gaza 

Blaha, who was the director of two different offices in the Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor in the state department from 2013 to 2023, said on Monday that his former employer "never officially explained its failure to enforce Leahy with regard to Israel, except to say that investigations are ongoing or cases are being reviewed".

"Behind the scenes, opponents of applying the law to Israel at the State Department and on the National Security Council have advanced specious, legally irrelevant policy arguments," he wrote.

Israel likely to lose Gaza genocide case if ICJ follows Myanmar ruling, Tel Aviv scholar says

Read More »

"During the Biden administration, Secretary of State Antony Blinken reportedly refused to implement Leahy with regard to Israel due to speculation that it would jeopardize unrelated ceasefire negotiations. The argument was far-fetched in 2024, and is obsolete now that Israel has signed the October 2025 Gaza peace plan."

The US has always had tools at its disposal to pressure allies to change direction, and especially ones who are dependent on US military assistance.

These tools include the Leahy Law, which prohibits US military assistance to units that violate human rights laws; the Export Control Act, which bars the transfer of weapons abroad if they could end up threatening US national security; and section 620I of the Foreign Assistance Act, which stipulates that the US government cannot provide weapons to a government that is hindering access to humanitarian aid. 

The Export Control Act, in particular, states that countries can only receive US weapons if they use them defensively, not offensively. 

Former state department official Hala Rharrit previously told Middle East Eye that its precisely why Blinken deferred to the refrain that “Israel has a right to defend itself”.

“It's not by accident [that] the words that [came] out of his mouth,” she said.

Loopholes

In December 2024, a month before the Biden administration left power, five Palestinians living in the US and Gaza filed a lawsuit against Blinken over accusations that Washington was not abiding by the Leahy Law and therefore allowing Israel to carry out its unprecedented assault on Gaza. 

That assault has since been assessed to be a genocide by both the United Nations and Holocaust scholars. More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since 7 October 2023, with at least 10,000 more missing under the rubble, the Lancet medical journal previously estimated. 

The lawsuit, which was filed with the help of the rights group Democracy for the Arab World Now (Dawn), outlined how the Biden administration created loopholes that allowed Israel to continue committing human rights violations without a suspension of aid from Washington.

One such loophole was the state department's establishment of the "Israel Leahy Vetting Forum", which the lawsuit said was designed "to impede any prompt and effective determination that Israeli units have committed" gross violations of human rights.

Dawn was founded by the late MEE columnist Jamal Khashoggi. One of the plaintiffs in the lawsuit is Gaza-born Ahmed Moor, who is running for the US Senate in 2028.

Blaha, who is now a senior adviser to Dawn, said in 2024 that "the standard for ineligibility is almost impossibly high" when it comes to Israel. 

"A determination that any Israeli unit is Leahy-ineligible rests with the deputy secretary of state. This is true for no other country in the world," he said. "Such determinations are routinely made at the working level, by experts versed in the Leahy Law and knowledgeable about the foreign security units in question."

The underlying culprit, he added, "is lack of political will".

US special envoy Jared Kushner pictured last week (Hannah McKay/AFP)

Israel is on track to become a “global pariah” over its genocide in the Gaza Strip, Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and diplomatic envoy, said in an interview released on Monday.

“Israel could rise from the tragedy of October 7, [and] be much more secure and much more integrated into the world, or they can go on the current trajectory, which is to trend toward global-pariah status,” Kushner said in an interview with New York Magazine.

The remarks are notable given Kushner’s longtime advocacy for Israel and efforts to put it at the centre of a new regional security architecture in the Middle East.

Kushner is a longtime family friend of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and created the controversial Board of Peace which was supposed to oversee Gaza’s reconstruction.

It is not clear what motivated Kushner’s comments, but his bid to be a Middle East peacemaker and builder has not held up, with Israel attacking the besieged enclave and much hyped-up reconstruction projects stalled.

The enclave was pummelled by Israel in a genocide of Palestinians after the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attack on southern Israel.

More than 70,000 Palestinians were killed in the onslaught with 1,679 people killed in Israeli strikes since the October 2025 “ceasefire” Kushner helped broker was announced.

The UN estimates it will cost $70bn to rebuild Gaza, but Kushner has struggled to launch even a small $2.45bn rebuilding project involving 66 projects across the enclave. Kushner blamed "different delays on different things, for whatever reason", during a presentation on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York City in September.

But the Gulf states have withheld funding and now face economic contractions because of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Middle East Eye revealed in May that Aryeh Lightstone, one of the key US officials overseeing the US’s post-war planning for Gaza, went to Saudi Arabia in the spring to lobby for funding but returned empty handed.

The much discussed international stabilisation force has not entered the territory and the Palestinian technocrats supposed to run day-to-day affairs also remain in Cairo.

The Times of Israel reported that “less than 2 percent” of the $17bn in pledges the Board of Peace was given have been met. In a sign of the board’s desperation, senior envoy Nickolay Mladenov travelled to Moscow on Monday and said Russia could contribute as a permanent member of the UN Security Council.

articles.title: Britain must stand firm against Nusseibeh's UN candidacy
articles.summary:
Britain must stand firm against Nusseibeh's UN candidacy

Submitted by
David Hearst
on
Tue, 11/24/2026 - 18:13

Appointing her as secretary general would effectively put the UAE and Israel, two nations determined to fuel regional chaos, in charge of the United Nations

Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh addresses the United Nations General Assembly in New York on 27 September 2025 (Charly Triballeau/AFP)

Off

For as long as anyone can remember, US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have used every platform to attack the United Nations, and every opportunity to defund its life-saving institutions.

Netanyahu called the UN a “swamp of antisemitism” that had to be drained. 

Trump called the UN Human Rights Council “craven hypocrites” who had little to say about the persecution of Christians, and accused Unesco - with its “ceaseless promotion of mass migration” - of actively destroying the greatest culture in history (ie the US).

Long before Israel claimed, without proof, that the UN Relief and Works Agency (Unrwa) was infiltrated by Hamas, Trump withdrew funding from Unrwa, cutting off the only UN agency dedicated specifically to Palestinian refugees.

How curious, then, that so much effort is being put into placing their candidate as the next secretary general of the UN.

Their candidate is Lana Nusseibeh, a British-educated diplomat from an old Palestinian family, who served as the UAE’s permanent representative to the UN from 2013 to 2024.

During those years, the country she represented actively worked against everything the UN was trying to do to stabilise the Middle East and Africa.

The Emirati network

The UAE funded a military coup in Egypt. In Libya, it ran guns, armoured vehicles and surveillance equipment in a constant airlift to the renegade general Khalifa Haftar in Benghazi and Tobruk, despite a UN arms embargo. 

Between April and July 2025, more than 30 military Il-76 flights were recorded between the UAE and Benghazi, some of which were operated by private firms contracted by Abu Dhabi.

Alongside the Egyptian military, the UAE plotted the downfall of parliamentary democracy in Tunisia. In Sudan, it has provided arms shipments, intelligence and logistics to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). It established two airfields - Berbera in breakaway Somaliland, and Bosaso in Puntland - to act as logistics hubs.

The UAE is attempting to leverage conflict and separatism in Libya, Sudan and the Horn of Africa, to project its power and economic influence without a territorial footprint. It acts mainly through proxies.

The objective is to position Abu Dhabi as a key security player and economic partner at strategic ports and global trade chokepoints, without the appearance of a traditional military footprint

During this campaign, the UN has been at the forefront of bringing the atrocities committed by UAE proxies to light. UN agencies have published a series of reports on ethnic cleansing by the RSF, the UAE’s primary actor in Sudan, which Abu Dhabi arms and bankrolls. 

Last year, the UN Human Rights Office published details of widespread killings, rape, torture and abductions committed during a three-day RSF offensive on the Zamzam displacement camp, which killed more than 1,000 civilians.

This past February, the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan found all the hallmarks of genocide in the RSF’s 500-day siege and sacking of El Fasher, the capital of North Darfur.

The sum effect of the UAE’s campaign in the Middle East and Africa can be measured in the latest World Food Programme (WFP) report on global famine. The UAE and Israel are fighting and fomenting strife in three of the five countries whose populations are identified by the WFP as facing catastrophe and risk of famine - Gaza, Nigeria, South Sudan, Yemen and Sudan. The conflicts it backs are the key drivers of famine, displacement and refugees.

The WFP, one of the main providers of food in Gaza, recently had to cut aid by a third, because it received half as much funding this year for its operations in Palestine.

Denying the undeniable

Put another way, the UAE exports more than just oil and gas. In Sudan alone, its exports amount to 19.5 million people facing acute hunger, and millions of others either internally displaced or fleeing to Chad, South Sudan, Egypt, Ethiopia or the Central African Republic.

The UAE’s covert interventions are highly structured, never ad hoc. And they are interlinked: supply routes through Chad and Libya have been used to arm the RSF in Sudan since April 2023, UN experts found, while the UAE has also shipped in mercenaries from Colombia.

The objective is to position Abu Dhabi as a key security player and economic partner at strategic ports and global trade chokepoints, without the appearance of a traditional military footprint. 

Who is Lana Nusseibeh, the UAE diplomat in the race to become next UN secretary-general?

Read More »

Almost everything it does is deniable - and it was Nusseibeh’s role for 11 years at the UN to keep it that way. Her second task was to forge ties with Israel, turning the Emiratis into Israel’s strongest diplomatic and military ally in the Arab world - far more important than the two Arab states with negotiated peace deals, Jordan and Egypt.

Netanyahu is a natural partner for UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed. Both think political Islam is an existential enemy. Mohammed bin Zayed is obsessed by the reach of the Muslim Brotherhood, believing it has power far beyond Egypt, its country of origin.

If Mohammed bin Zayed’s cohort of dictators saw the Arab Spring in Tunisia, Egypt and Yemen as a personal threat, the Emirati ruler saw it also as an ideological one.

In his jihad against political Islam, Mohammed bin Zayed sees the Brotherhood everywhere, ascribing to it a presence and a role far greater than it actually possesses. He sees the Brotherhood in London, Paris and Berlin - and the Emiratis are hard at work funding and tutoring the racist European far right in Islamophobia. 

Reshaping the region

Outside Mohammed bin Zayed’s jihad, the truth about the Muslim Brotherhood is ironically quite different.

While the movement is organisationally at its weakest, after decades of oppression and imprisonment in Egypt, Jordan and Tunisia, Israel’s genocide in Gaza helped political Islam recover to an extent not thought possible just a few years ago.

The Gaza genocide has lowered the barriers between political Islam and the secular left - barriers once so high that they fatally weakened the first wave of democratic revolution in Egypt and Tunisia for more than a decade.

The key distinction in the diaspora now is less whether you are secular or Islamist, but whether you are active or passive in organising against genocide.

Can anyone imagine what Israel would do to the UN, and to all those fact-finding reports and investigations bubbling away inside, with its own candidate running the institution?

Both the UAE and Israel have big ambitions to “reshape” the Middle East, away from the dominance of traditional nation states. Both are small countries, dwarfed in population and land by larger neighbours, and their aim is to dominate as technological and military hubs by splitting up the others.

Israel says this openly about Syria, and allows academics to speculate about dismembering Egypt. The UAE is only too happy to encourage these plans, because its principal target is its lumbering neighbour, Saudi Arabia. 

Both Israel and the UAE are avid users of mobile phone software to spy on and target dissidents abroad. 

Pro-Israel lobbying groups are too quick to recognise the importance of Nusseibeh’s work and reward her for it. In a revealing column, Jake Wallis Simons, former editor of the Jewish Chronicle, said he preferred an Emirati Palestinian over a progressive Jew from Costa Rica, Rebeca Grynspan - as if the choice of secretary general boiled down to ethnicity.

True, everything that happens in Israel is ruled by ethnicity. Even Zionist Arabs are discarded as potential partners for government by the opposition leaders desperate to get rid of Netanyahu. 

But happily, racism outside the pariah state has not yet descended to those depths.

Not a shoo-in

Unusually, with the backers she has secured, Nusseibeh is not a shoo-in for the top UN job. 

There have now been nine “straw polls”, or informal soundings of the permanent and elected members of the Security Council, to determine who should replace Antonio Guterres as secretary general. Although these votes are cast anonymously, the UK, France and China, all permanent members, are believed to have voted against Nusseibeh. 

In the latest poll on Friday, Nusseibeh received seven “encourage” votes, six “discourage” votes, and two “no opinion” votes - the same result she achieved on 6 November.

The process is opaque, and until now, no permanent member has formally cast a veto. But the selection of a successor appears deadlocked.

China is an advocate of the principle of rotation, and therefore favours a candidate from Latin America, but the reluctance of the UK and France to sign on the dotted line was unexpected.

No one needs a UN report to tell them what is happening in Sudan or Yemen. 

The military defeats of western alliances in the last six interventions in the Middle East and Central Asia, should not lead anyone to rashly assume that the ideology of intervention has been abandoned. It’s simply easier all around to sell the franchise to Israel and the UAE. 

At the same time, Abu Dhabi has been hard at work selling the myth that it represents the “model Arab” state of the future: a lip gloss of social liberalism covering a hard-baked, technologically cutting-edge dictatorship. 

Not even Iran’s missiles and drones have punctured the myth that it’s “business as usual” again in Dubai and Abu Dhabi. The financial incentives for Britain to look the other way are enormous, when all that blood gold, and those blood diamonds from Africa, are laundered on their way to Moscow.

Lobbying pressure

Britain is locked in a tight embrace with the UAE. Some 250,000 expat Britons work in Dubai and Abu Dhabi. More than 5,000 British companies work in the Emirates as a whole. The UAE holds nearly £30bn ($39bn) of investment pledges in more than 50 deals. 

Apart from Manchester City, it owns P&O Ferries, and holds an eight percent stake in Gatwick Airport. It also has stakes in the broadband provider CityFibre, parts of Berkeley Square in central London, and a major regeneration project in Manchester.

In the twilight years of neoliberalism, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham finds that his country has already flogged the Emiratis anything that was not nailed down, and much that was. 

The biggest brake on Burnham changing anything radically in the relationship between Britain and its colonial creation is being applied by the Treasury, not the Foreign Office - although there are many there who are still in love with the UAE model.

Nusseibeh's first task would be to kill off the only international mechanism the world has left to calm things down, reintroduce stability and resolve conflicts

The UK’s presumed veto in the straw polls has put ferocious lobbying pressure on Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband. 

The lobbying campaign for Nusseibeh has been relentless and wide-ranging. She came to visit former Conservative Party leader Iain Duncan Smith at his office in Westminster after he spoke out in parliament against the UAE’s involvement in Sudan and her candidacy.

Duncan Smith denounced the UAE’s “sponsoring of a huge amount of terrorism in Sudan”, and called on Britain to use its Security Council veto to block her nomination.

Interestingly, Nusseibeh reportedly did not deny to Duncan Smith that her country was funding and bankrolling the RSF.

Nusseibeh’s supporters in the UK wax lyrical about the qualities and energy of the 48-year-old diplomat.

“She’s charming. She’s extremely eloquent. She’s a fast thinker. She’s the best diplomat I’ve ever met,” one former British diplomat told Middle East Eye. “She’s assertive, and so she’s been good at articulating the UAE’s foreign policy position, which is that it has a right to be assertive.”

And, of course, she was educated at Wycombe Abbey and Cambridge - so that’s all right, then.

One source who spoke to the Financial Times said the choice was between principle and pragmatism. But that is exactly where the UK is going wrong. 

Global recovery

Miliband and Burnham should be preparing the UK for the post-Trump era. 

Today, it is funny to be a racist bigot in Israel. Elon Musk thinks it's a good look to throw the weight of his satellites around politics in the US and Ukraine, and into space, like some 16th-century buccaneer on a mission to discover the New World.

But in a very short time, today’s testosterone-fuelled, ego-driven strongman act is going to look so dated, and so ill-suited to the state the world is actually in. The neoliberal legacy, honed to extremes by Trump and his oligarchs, will be a weaker global economy, no real international order, and a chaos buffeted regularly by war, climate shocks and economic crashes.

The world will need a long period in which to recover, if indeed it ever does. It will have to rediscover the need for strong international institutions to feed populations, keep the peace, and rebuild postwar landscapes across the Middle East, Ukraine and Africa. 

Why Britain must oppose UN candidacy of UAE's Nusseibeh

Read More »

It will need international rules and courts to adjudicate those rules, not nations that tear those rules up. The International Criminal Court and International Court of Justice will need to work around the clock. 

The world will not need international courts cut down to size to protect war criminals in the US or Israel. 

Putting Nusseibeh in place as secretary general would be to put her paymasters - the UAE and Israel - in charge of the UN. 

These are the very pariah states that are actively working to spread conflict around the Middle East and Africa, and to subvert the institutions of the UN and international law for their own gain. 

Israel is starving Gaza by keeping UN agencies at the Egyptian border, and bombing aid workers inside the territory. Can anyone imagine what Israel would do to the UN, and to all those fact-finding reports and investigations bubbling away inside, with its own candidate running the institution?

Nusseibeh’s first task would be to kill off the only international mechanism the world has left to calm things down, reintroduce stability and resolve conflicts.  

It is pragmatism, not just principle, to oppose such a takeover. Britain, as a veto-wielding member of the Security Council, must hold firm.

articles.title: US judge permanently bars Trump from punishing rights groups who liaise with ICC
articles.summary:
US judge permanently bars Trump from punishing rights groups who liaise with ICC

Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Tue, 11/24/2026 - 16:42

The president's executive order had put several US-based organisations at risk of fines and prison time

The International Criminal Court in The Hague (Remko De Waal/ANP/AFP)

Off

A US federal judge on Monday permanently barred the Trump administration from punishing rights groups who liaise with the International Criminal Court (ICC).

The ruling extends to all Americans, and not just the plaintiffs in the case.

Judge Jesse Furman of the Southern District of New York first issued a temporary injunction last month.

This week he ruled that while "the Government effectively requests that the Court reconsider its earlier decisions ... there is no merit to that request".

"Put simply, Plaintiffs demonstrate that the Services Prohibition is a content-based restriction on speech and that it is not narrowly tailored to serve compelling state interests," Furman wrote. 

Democracy for the Arab World Now (Dawn), founded by the late Middle East Eye columnist Jamal Khashoggi, filed the lawsuit in July.

In October, Furman blocked the Trump administration from potentially imposing civil or criminal liability on the group as well as another allied organisation, the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (Taag), for any work carried out with the ICC. 

"Anyone violating this prohibition could face up to 20 years in prison and up to $1 million in civil fines," Dawn said in a press release on Tuesday.

"Because the government can interpret the term 'services' to encompass anything that confers a benefit on the recipient, Americans before this ruling risked criminal prosecution for submitting evidence about possible crimes to the ICC, or for exchanging information with and engaging in joint advocacy with the Palestinian human rights groups and Special Rapporteur [Francesca] Albanese."

US judge bars Trump from punishing rights groups for liaising with ICC

Read More »

Albanese, the United Nations special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories, has been sanctioned by the Trump administration since 2025.

"The permanent injunction strips the Trump administration of one of its most expansive tools - the power to jail or impose crippling fines on Americans for assisting the ICC and for working with groups who were sanctioned for demanding accountability for US and Israeli atrocity crimes - just weeks after the administration sanctioned the entire ICC," Dawn said.

"The court has affirmed that every American has the constitutional right to advocate for justice on Palestine without fear of reprisal."

Both Dawn and Taag confirmed they "will immediately move forward with ... ICC work and resume working closely with Special Rapporteur Albanese and the sanctioned Palestinian civil society groups". 

Two weeks ago, Taag held a press conference at The Hague calling on the ICC to investigate Trump and his top diplomat Marco Rubio for "aiding and abetting genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity committed by Israel in Gaza".

US versus the ICC

In the early weeks of his presidency some 18 months ago, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14203, granting US officials the power to impose sanctions on foreigners for supporting the ICC's investigations into US and Israeli nationals for war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide.

He made it a federal offence to provide a "service" to, or receive one from, a sanctioned individual or entity.

ICC investigations, the Trump administration said, constitute a "national emergency" because the ICC lacks jurisdiction over crimes committed by US and Israeli nationals during wartime. 

While Washington played a role in the early development of the ICC and signed the Rome Statute in 2000 under the presidency of Bill Clinton, it never submitted the statute to the Senate for ratification, amid fears that the ICC could prosecute US military personnel and officials for alleged war crimes, especially in conflicts in Afghanistan and Iraq. 

Trump himself has been blunt about needing to punish the ICC for specifically going after Israel. 

Using Executive Order 14203, Trump has so far sanctioned ICC prosecutors and judges, as well as the Palestinian human rights groups al-Haq, al-Mezan and the Palestinian Centre for Human Rights.

articles.title: Zelenskyy summarises meeting with Hungarian PM: energy, trade and support discussed

We also spoke about humanitarian demining and expanding Hungary's participation in the relevant Coalition. Concrete agreements have been reached on all these issues."
